#3592. How the Newly Elected Congress Can Save the Smithsonian

This is the November 6, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors. The Democrats have flipped the House and the Senate, which could usher in a new era of funding at the Smithsonian—or, at the very least, a vibe shift in DC. There are a ton of gallery shows opening around New York, and on the West Coast, LACMA Art+Film Gala goes down tomorrow night. We got the rare chance to sit down with one of the night’s honorees, Vija Celmins.

Mentioned in this issue: Donald Trump, Lonnie Bunch, Alma Allen, Tilman Fertitta, Yoshitomo Nara, Loïc Gouzer, Vija Celmins, Matthew Marks, Leonardo DiCaprio, Eva Chow, Denis Villeneuve, Gary Hume, Jacqueline Tran, Michael Govan, Katherine Ross, James Turrell, Riko Mizuno, Matthew Barney, Roni Horn, Meshell Ndegeocello, Steve McQueen, Matthieu Blazy, Rosemarie Trockel, Carrie Mae Weems, Marina Abramović, Wade Guyton, Christopher Wool, Rashid Johnson, Felix Rödder, Calvin Marcus, James Ensor.

Trump has spent the last two years attacking Washington’s cultural hub with executive orders and legally dubious firings issued via fiat. But the Smithsonian gets its funding through Congress—what if Congress actually acted on that authority?

Sure, Congress has more pressing issues to address once the deeply blue House and Senate get sworn in early next year. But here at True Colors I think it’s fair to ask the question: Will lawmakers wind back the years of impact the Trump administration has had on the Smithsonian Institution?

Although Congress has authority over the cultural behemoth, the White House has in just the last two years issued executive orders, been extremely hands-on in its public signage, and mounted pressure campaigns to fire directors and censor artworks. Congress could have stopped all of this, but didn't. Republicans naturally didn’t want to cross Trump and support the beleaguered arts mecca. But Democrats have every reason to—after the new Congress is sworn in they’ll have the power to appropriate massive amounts of funding to each Smithsonian museum—or even create new museums. Plus, that can impact how the whole institution is run on a day-to-day basis, as Congress has the power to shake up the Smithsonian’s board of regents. That governing body will choose the next Smithsonian secretary, after Lonnie Bunch resigned earlier this year.

I’m particularly interested in who takes over as the director of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. Melissa Chiu, who held the position for 12 years, stepped down earlier this year to be the director of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and rumors are swirling about who will succeed her in the post. The prospect of a culture-living Congress—and, who knows...a Democratic president come 2029?—could make the Smithsonian seem like a swell place to be long term.

Add in the prospect of a new crop of congressional staffers and the attendant cottage industries of consultants and lobbyists all flocking to Washington, and I could see the Hirshhorn getting caught up in the vibe shift, pronto. There’s expected to be a sea change of DC residents in town, and there’s every reason to believe they’ll make the (free! always free!) contemporary art museum a constant stop on the rotation. Plus, the long-gestating renovation of the Sculpture Garden literally just opened this past weekend. I don’t have any inside intel on who’s in the running for the job —but it’s looking like a pretty great gig these days.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Meanwhile, the artworks that filled the American Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, made by State Department–tapped artist Alma Allen, might be stuck in Italy for the foreseeable future. Funding has run out, and there’s nothing in the budget for moving the works. I wonder how that can be resolved. Seems like a job for an art-loving, restaurant-owning Italian ambassador, Tilman Fertitta!

The massive two-location Yoshitomo Nara show opened at David Zwirner last night, truly one of the great gallery moments here in New York this season. Don’t miss the pop-up one-painting exhibition of Nara’s In the Milky Lake / Thinking One, which will be sold by Loïc Gouzer’s one-lot auction business, Fair Warning. It’s on view at 534 W. 22nd Street. The lot opens for live bidding November 19 and is expected to sell for the eye-popping sum of $10 million to $15 million.

You can also see Nara’s work in Washington, DC, where the aforementioned Hirshhorn just opened a grand survey of the artist timed to the inauguration of its sculpture garden. And if you want to check out some of Nara’s artworks in a very unexpected place, head to the Avenue A dive bar Niagara, where Nara drunkenly created a masterwork on the walls late one night after an opening at Pace. The bar wisely conserved the artwork behind glass, and it remains there nearly two decades later.

It’s not usually worth reporting on the toasts given at gala dinners here in the prized real estate that is this newspaper’s Table Hopping section, but the Dia Fall Night had some good honorary toast content! On Monday, Matthew Barney proved himself to be a very deep Roni Horn fan with his toast. Then Meshell Ndegeocello went super outside the box, honoring Steve McQueen by stepping in front of the podium and leading a band around the gala. The whole evening was like that. Chanel wasn’t just a sponsor—the brand’s creative director Matthieu Blazy, a true contemporary art head, chaired the whole thing alongside artists Rosemarie Trockel and Carrie Mae Weems. Marina Abramović was at my table; she told me she reads Vanity Fair every time she’s on a plane and appreciates how thick the issues have been lately. Marina, it’s an honor. Thank you for reading.

Matthew Marks hosted a party on Wednesday night for Wade Guyton’s excellent new show at Bridges, the best restaurant on Chatham Square. Fun fact: Christopher Wool’s old studio was right next to the restaurant some decades back.

On Election Day, as the results started coming in, Rashid Johnson opened a show of new work at Hauser & Wirth’s Wooster Street gallery, which has recently become my favorite of the mega-gallery’s dozen or so global outposts. It’s a throwback of sorts, a small space in the neighborhood that was once the city’s gallery nexus, with an excellent track record of great shows. The dinner was at the gallery’s restaurant, Manuela, right around the corner on Prince Street. There was caviar, and while it was served to celebrate Johnson, it happened to come out right as the news networks indicated the Democrats were going to flip a Senate seat in South Carolina. Spirits were high.

If you’re making your way to The Met to see “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” do stop by Rodder, the gallery founded by Felix Rödder, to see one of the most inspired artist pairings in the city right now. Calvin Marcus, the fanatically talented and free-wheeling Los Angeles painter, has new and recent paintings, drawings, and ceramics installed alongside work by the great Belgian weirdo James Ensor. The chemistry between these two artists from different centuries and continents is uncanny. The dinner for the show was held somewhere unusual: House of the Redeemer, the Episcopalian Church in a former Italian Renaissance Revival townhouse once owned by a Vanderbilt heiress.

#3591. Both Sizes of the Latest M5 MacBook Air Are $200 Off Right Now

Apple announced a slew of products in March that ended up increasing in price later in June due to the RAM shortage, including the MacBook Air with the M5 chip. These MacBooks come in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: Amazon is selling both right now at a $200 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,299 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes, according to tracking tools.

The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people in 2026, as they usually are with every new model when it comes to value for your money. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Airs, the M5 base model has double the storage at 512GB. The M5 chip is powerful and makes the performance even smoother, according to Mashable's review. The aluminum design is as good as you'd expect from Apple's most popular portable laptop, keeping it lightweight and thin. It comes with a Liquid Retina display, Touch ID, a 12MP Center Stage Camera, and the Magic Keyboard.

Typically, the question would be whether to go for the slightly older M4 MacBook Air or pay a bit more for the newer M5 chip—but given how tough it is to find a new M4 laptop and that most refurbished ones are the same price as the M5 with 512GB of storage, it makes the choice to go with the M5 a no-brainer—especially with the $200 discount.

Boreanaz is once again playing a PI... This time without the fangs.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I think we can all agree when it comes to David Boreanaz, the man never misses. Whether it’s a vampire with a soul, a witty FBI agent, or even a Navy SEAL, he has given each generation their own Boreanaz to love. Now he’s tackling a reboot that is brimming with nostalgia, and bringing him back into PI work. Only this time he's doing it without the fangs, and it has me very excited, especially since he received the blessing of James Garner’s daughter. The actor’s The Rockford Files is finally becoming real thanks to NBC’s fun new look.

The network just dropped a delightful (and unique) promo on their Instagram for the upcoming PI series in the form of an ad. It even has a number you can call now: 1-760-JIM-ROCK. It definitely feels like something from the ‘70s when the show was on air. Plus, Boreanaz taking off the sunglasses to make his point feels very Rockford, but the ad itself says it all:

Whether it’s identity theft, infidelity, embezzlement, extortion. If you got questions, I’ll find you answers. Jim Rockford. Private Investigator. Let’s roll.

First off, the vibes were also given me a procedural from the ‘80s. The sunny backdrop and the private investigator here to help pitch reminded me of the Magnum PI reboot in all the best ways. The reboot also did a two season stint on NBC. This has made me even more excited to check out the new series… possibly even more than his Angel/Buffy co-star Charisma Carpenter. The "ad" is also giving a little tease to what we can expect plot wise.

According to NBC, the show follows Rockford “a private investigator who is newly paroled after serving time for a crime he did not commit.” This is a similar premise to the original series in which Jim Rockford did five years for a crime he didn’t commit before being patrolled. If this makes you go "oooh," then you should also check out the series RJ Decker which follows an ex-con who becomes a PI after being railroaded and serving time in prison.

However, I’m not the only one who thinks the Rockford vibes totally slay. Fans have sounded off in the comments, particularly about Boreanaz’s full circle career and resemblance to Garner:

Turns out, Boreanaz’s mother was right when she told him that he looked like Garner. Thankfully he listened. At least this time he shouldn’t need a stake. But is there any chance we’ll see some of his past co-stars as clients? I’m still holding onto hope for a potential Bones reunion someday, but I will settle for a Buffy/Angel one.

However, while he seems to be nailing the role in the promo, fans were initially unsure about him taking on the project. They can rest easy knowing that Boreanaz is doing his best to honor Garner’s legacy while offering something new with the character.

We can all find out just how much Boreanaz nails the part when the series premieres on January 2 with a special preview. It can be watched the next day with a Peacock subscription, and you bet I will be watching.

#3589. Godzilla Minus Zero's King Ghidorah Has One Scene That Was 55 Years In The Making

This article contains minor spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is here, with director Takashi Yamazaki once again getting to put his stamp on the King of the Monsters. He also got to offer up his take on another classic kaiju this time around in the form of King Ghidorah. The monster's appearance was a poorly kept secret, with Ghidorah's design in "Godzilla Minus Zero" leaking thanks to merchandise. But in any event, the monster's inclusion helped resolve a 55-year-old dream for the filmmaker.

According to Reuters, Yamazaki grew up in the Japanese ‌city of Matsumoto. A big "Godzilla" fan, he was particularly excited about 1964's "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time. In particular, he hoped to see the kaiju wreck shop in his hometown. Unfortunately, Matsumoto only appeared fleetingly in the movie after Ghidorah's emergence.

Given that "Godzilla Minus One" became the highest-grossing Japanese Godzilla movie ever en route to winning an Oscar, Yamazaki was given a lot of creative freedom on the sequel. He used that freedom to show Ghidorah doing what he wanted to see as a child. "Minus Zero" prominently features Matsumoto, with Ghidorah carving a path of destruction there relatively early on in the movie's runtime. Here's what the filmmaker had to say about it:

"55 years later, I had King ‌Ghidorah ​appear in my own film. I had the chance ⁠to make the movie I ⁠wanted to watch back then, and I created the footage that I wanted to show my younger self, as if to say, 'This is what you wanted to see, isn't it?'"

"So, my dream has finally come true after ​55 years, and I am truly happy," Takashi Yamazaki concluded.

The sequel picks up two years after the events of "Minus One" as Japan is still trying to put itself back together in the aftermath of Godzilla's attacks. Things are once again thrown into chaos when a new, mysterious, dragon-like monster emerges. It's not long before Godzilla is back as well, leaving the people of Japan scrambling to figure out how to deal with not one but two kaiju.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is rated R, which meant that Yamazaki didn't have to hold back at all. When it came to having King Ghidorah destroy his hometown, he certainly made the most of that R rating. In a bizarre method of showing pride for the place he came from, he made the most of Matsumoto in his latest cinematic effort. Being from Japan and having your home shown off in a "Godzilla" movie is, understandably, something to be proud of.

King Ghidorah was the movie's "surprise" villain who has a long history with the franchise. "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" was his first of many, many appearances across the many eras of this franchise. In recent years, he's been showcased in everything from "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" in the MonsterVerse to the animated "Godzilla: The Planet Eater" on Netflix. He's without a doubt Godzilla's most notorious foe.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3588. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

#3587. 10 Devastating Game Cancellations That Are Still Disappointing Years Later

The best games ever — from an alternate timeline

Sometimes, it’s fun to think about the great games that might have been — until they were canceled without ever getting the chance to make their mark. Most of the time, we just shrug our shoulders and move on, because that’s life. But sometimes, we mourn the wasted potential.

Some of those canceled games might have fought the odds and disappointed us anyway, like Duke Nukem Forever. Others might just as easily have become massive hits, if only they had been allocated additional time and resources. In that regard, they’re a bit like Schrodinger’s cat. With both possible outcomes in mind, here are the 10 canceled games we’re still upset about years later. They could have been contenders!

Players looking forward to a shooter set in the StarCraft universe had twelve years to hope and dream before finally having to accept that nothing was ever going to come of StarCraft: Ghost. First announced in 2002, the title spent several years in active development before being placed on indefinite hold in 2006. Over the course of those years, the industry changed a lot. For that matter, so did the development team. Although there has been a lot of discussion about what went wrong with StarCraft: Ghost, the game’s eventual cancellation was due to numerous factors. Perhaps the biggest of them was the success of a different Blizzard property: World of Warcraft. We can easily understand why Blizzard management would have chosen to allocate resources toward a property that was red-hot at the time. Even so, it stings a little that StarCraft didn’t get its spinoff.

Electronic Arts, who would have been the one to publish Dead Space 4, technically never announced it. Years later, we only know the game was in development because some of the developers responsible have said so. Originally, it began development in February of 2013, following the launch of Dead Space 3. That previous game clearly didn’t sell as well as Electronic Arts hoped. Since the writing was on the wall, leadership chose to have Visceral focus on other projects. Dead Space 4 development ended not long after it began, and well before any playable levels could be built. The development studio itself followed in 2017. As for the franchise, it seems to be done for, especially after the terrific Dead Space remake failed to expand its audience.

History has proven that games can be all but finished and still get canceled. Such was the case for Fable Legends, a multiplayer action-RPG that was preparing for its open beta phase at the time of its cancellation in 2016. First revealed at Gamescom in 2013, the game spent around four years in development. Developer Lionhead Studios had just finished Fable Journey and said goodbye to co-founder Peter Molyneux when it went to work on a new action-RPG intended to showcase the power of the Xbox One. A live service game might not seem like the right fit for a studio known for its single-player prowess, but Microsoft executives knew best and they were willing to spend piles of money to make their vision a reality. When the game’s development finally ended in 2016, just shy of a proper release, so did Lionhead Studios.

The California Raisins: The Grape Escape came about as close to releasing as a game can without entering the manufacturing process, then dropped out of sight at the last minute. If you read old gaming magazines, you’ll sometimes find pictures of the familiar dried fruit mascot in sunglasses, forcing its way around a plump bunch of grapes. But the ads and all references to the game disappeared overnight. One possible reason for the abrupt change is the fact that the raisins and their crooning style were already on their way out of fashion. Capcom also had other big projects to tend to. For context, 1990 is the same year it released Mega Man 3 and Gargoyle’s Quest in North America, along with numerous arcade titles. Besides that, the Super Nintendo was fast approaching. But at least for fans of the raisins, there’s good news: someone found a prototype cart and dumped its contents all over the internet. If you want to see what the game was all about, you technically can, even though it never got its flowers.

In 2006, we learned that we could look forward to playing Star Wars Battlefront 3, this time from Free Radical Design instead of Pandemic Studios. Then in late 2008, we learned that we shouldn’t look forward to it at all when LucasArts canceled the project. During the time it spent on the game, the team reportedly produced a build that was nearly final. Unfortunately, Free Radical Design and LucasArts couldn’t reach an agreement to carry that third installment across the finish line and serve it up to players. Then, in 2016, an Xbox 360 prototype leaked. It provided a glimpse of how the game might have played, had it been released. Next, a fully playable Wii build of Star Wars Battlefront 3 materialized in late 2024. We finally got to see what we had missed. Sadly, nothing could give us back the 16 years we had to live without that experience.

Game engines are supposed to simplify the development process, but they don’t always achieve that result. Unreal Engine 4 enabled some amazing games to come to fruition, but it didn’t streamline things for the team at PlatinumGames, which wrestled with the engine and ultimately failed to deliver Scalebound to Microsoft. First announced at E3 in 2014, the promising game was scheduled to arrive in 2016. Then it slipped into the next year and finally was canceled when the developer failed to produce a stable, playable piece of software. Perhaps the ambitious team, led by Hideki Kamiya of Bayonetta fame, simply tried to do more than its resources permitted. Maybe there were other less interesting problems. Whatever the case, the game never happened and probably never will. That’s a shame. The story of a boy and his dragon is one we would have liked to see.

There must be something about Star Wars, because two games from that franchise found their way to this list. Star Wars 1313 was to be an action-adventure game focusing on everyone’s favorite bounty hunter, Boba Fett. Handled internally at LucasArts, the title spent roughly three years in development. When Disney acquired LucasArts in late 2012, there was still a ways to go. Unfortunately, the new owners weren’t interested in paying to provide the necessary runway, especially not after investing more than $4 billion to buy the company. They canceled the project around six months later, leaving us to mourn what might have been. The closest we’ll probably ever get to a Star Wars experience along similar lines is Ubisoft’s semi-recent release, Star Wars Outlaws.

Some publishers consider sales in excess of 1 million units a success, but Square Enix is not one of them. At least, it wasn’t when the title in question was Sleeping Dogs (previously set to be published by Activision as True Crime: Hong Kong). It presented an engaging environment that compared favorably to the likes of Ubisoft’s Watch Dogs, but it failed to meet sales projections. United Front Games then went to work on a sequel that would have expanded the story and offered two-player cooperative play, among other enhancements. Square Enix passed on the pitch, however, and encouraged the team to build the project that became Triad Wars… which only made it as far as a beta phase before it also got shut down. For United Front Games and the Sleeping Dogs franchise both, that cancellation marked the end of the line.

If you own a working PlayStation 4 with the demo of Silent Hills (originally known as P.T.) installed, you have a piece of history. First revealed in August 2014 as a playable teaser, the game’s development united Hideo Kojima (best known for Metal Gear Solid) and Hollywood horror director Guillermo del Toro. The happy pair planned to work with actor Norman Reedus to revitalize the popular Silent Hill horror franchise, which had fallen upon hard times. Eight months later, Konami canceled the game-in-progress and Kojima left the company to make Death Stranding (partnering with Reedus again). A few years later, Capcom presented a fresh take on Resident Evil with a seventh installment that reminded some players of P.T. As for Konami, it wasn’t done with Silent Hill. In fact, Silent Hill: Townfall, a promising new installment from No Code and Annapurna Interactive, is due next month.

Capcom didn’t quite have a massive hit with its two Mega Man Legends games (three if you count The Misadventures of Tron Bonne). Still, it had cultivated an audience that it decided to pursue with a third numbered installment. Announced as an early 3DS title in September 2010, Mega Man Legends 3 incorporated feedback from a community of Mega Man fans. Eager players voted on characters, designs, and mechanics as development progressed. When Capcom canceled the project in July of 2011, not long after Keiji Inafune left the company in late 2010, the move felt very abrupt. A demo was on its way, with multiple levels and a new protagonist, but it never got released. The 3DS recovered from its alarming weak launch and went on to become a genuinely successful platform, but the reversal of fortune came too late to spare the third installment in Capcom’s niche series. Its cancellation means the cliffhanger at the end of Mega Man Legends 2 remains unresolved to this day. Maybe Capcom will come back to the series in the future to explore what comes next, but we wouldn’t count on it. In the meantime, at least we have Mega Man: Dual Override to look forward to in 2027.

Hideki Kamiya hasn't given up on Scalebound

#3586. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, Apple TV, Hulu, And More (Nov. 6-8)

It's the first full weekend of November, the weather is finally turning truly chilly, and Halloweekend is in the rear-view mirror. Whether you went all-out on your costume last weekend or you elected to slap a nametag with a different moniker on your shirt and call it a day (which is my preferred way to celebrate Halloween if asked to do so), this weekend is perfect for staying in and curling up with a fresh series or movie. So, what's new on the big streamers?

Between Apple, Peacock, Hulu, and Netflix, there's a decent spate of new releases heading to streaming this weekend (and some of them even dropped earlier in the week). Whether you want to watch a gripping spy drama, a truly ridiculous legal drama, a breezy sports comedy, a crime thriller tinged with romance, or a quick-paced series featuring one of the best and weirdest pairings in TV history, I've got you covered.

Director Adam Carter Rehmeier, known for indie films like "Snack Shack" and "Dinner in America," teamed up with modern scream queen Samara Weaving and horror staple Kyle Gallner for this year's "Carolina Caroline" — which just hit Netflix, marking its first home on a major streaming service. Weaving, who also led "Ready or Not 2: Here I Come" and "Over Your Dead Body" recently (and who's joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe to play Emma Frost), stars as Caroline Daniels, a gas station attendant who falls in love with Gallner's con artist Oliver Anderson. As the two make their way to South Carolina from rural Texas, they end up committing robbery after robbery, leaving destruction in their wake.

Weaving's Caroline and Gallner's Oliver make for a great modern Bonnie and Clyde, and "Carolina Caroline" is a gripping, entertaining, and extraordinarily fun film that also features Jon Gries ("Napoleon Dynamite," "The White Lotus") and Kyra Sedgwick in supporting roles. If you want a crime drama packed with plenty of romance, "Carolina Caroline" on Netflix is your best bet.

Congratulations to all bad TV enjoyers: One of the worst shows ever made is back for Season 2! Ryan Murphy's gleefully ludicrous legal drama "All's Fair," which undoubtedly gives real lawyers raging headaches if they dare to tune in, stars Kim Kardashian as high-powered lawyer Allura Grant, who works alongside Liberty Ronson (Naomi Watts), Emerald J. Greene-Ball (Niecy Nash-Betts), Dina Standish (Glenn Close), and Milan (Teyana Taylor) at a firm that handles divorces. Sarah Paulson, a regular Murphy collaborator, livens up proceedings as rival lawyer Carrington "Carr" Lane, who is unbelievably twisted and extremely fun, and Nash-Betts, Watts, and Close are all game to ham it up.

I don't think I'm blowing anyone's mind when I say Kim Kardashian is a generationally dreadful actor who should not even appear in commercials, let alone a scripted drama that could be dishy and fun if she wasn't swanning around with absolutely zero expression in every single scene. Still, if you dig wildly bad TV and just want to switch your brain off, check out "All's Fair." Besides, if nothing else, it has given us an incredible episode of its fellow Hulu series "The Kardashians" where Close, out of character, gets very drunk off martinis at Kris Jenner's house.

I love "30 Rock," I have immense respect for weird little guy and short king Daniel Radcliffe, and I've been riding for Bobby Moynihan since the first time I saw him perform as Drunk Uncle on "Saturday Night Live." Essentially, "The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins" — which stars Tracy Morgan, was created by Robert Carlock and Sam Means, is executive produced by Tina Fey, and stars Morgan and Radcliffe as the unlikeliest and best duo in recent TV memory — was made for me in a lab. My enduring affection for this show aside, I think it's sure to delight pretty much anybody, and when Season 1 premiered in January, it immediately became one of the best shows of 2026.

The premise? Morgan plays Reggie Dinkins, a disgraced NFL star who was banned from the New York Jets and all other professional teams in the league after being caught betting on his games. (Hilariously, he only bet on his own performance to inspire himself to play better.) Thus, Reggie tries to regain his tattered reputation alongside his best friend and former teammate Rusty (Moynihan), his ex-wife and manager Monica (Erika Alexander), his young but extremely compatible fiancée Brina (Precious Joy), his son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall), and Radcliffe's Oscar-winning documentarian Arthur Tobin. With Arthur living in his palatial suburban New York mansion to make a documentary that will hopefully relaunch Reggie's career and get him into the NFL Hall of Fame, Reggie does his best to refurbish his image, and the results are extremely funny. "Reggie Dinkins" Season 2 dropped on NBC and Peacock on November 2, and if you're returning to this near-perfect series, welcome back. If you're new, go laugh your way through Season 1, then join us.

If you enjoyed Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw's delightful spy drama "Black Doves" when it dropped back on Netflix in 2024, you'll be pleased to hear the series — created by Joe Barton — released its second season on the streamer on November 5. Across six episodes, we pick up where the show left off with Helen Dawson (Knightley), a secret Black Doves operative who sells secrets to the highest bidder and also happens to be married to a Conservative MP for a major UK constituency and Secretary of State for Defense, Wallace Webb (Andrew Buchan). In the beginning of Season 1, Helen is shocked and saddened to learn that her lover, Jason Davies (Andre Koji), has died under suspicious circumstances ... and her secret identity may now be at risk.

Throughout that first season, Helen teams up with her old friend and hired assassin Sam Young (Whishaw), who's sent by the Doves to help protect her. In Season 2, after a shocking cliffhanger ending, we follow Helen and Sam as he desperately tries to keep her safe, even as she's targeted by nefarious forces throughout England. Knightley and Whishaw are fantastic together, and if you sort of forgot "Black Doves" was a thing since Season 1 premiered 2 years ago, I'm happy to tell you that it's back and still an extremely fun and enthralling watch.

Apple TV has some of the best comedy series on television hiding on its service (which seems to get overlooked in favor of ones like Netflix, Hulu, and Prime Video), and if you're a fan of "Ted Lasso" but haven't watched "Stick," you're really missing out. Owen Wilson leads this sports comedy created by Jason Keller and stars as Pryce Cahill, a former golf pro nicknamed "The Stick" who's stuck selling clubs and coaching at a country club after years of a career decline. At work one day, Pryce meets a gifted young golfer, Santi Wheeler (Peter Dager), who quit golfing after some personal issues got in the way of his game. Determined to make Santi the next golf star, Pryce ends up roping him into a cross-country tour to show off his talents alongside Santi's mother Elena (Mariana Treviño), Pryce's former caddy Mitts (Marc Maron), and a onetime bartender and current caddy Zero Duffy (Lili Kay), all of whom pile into an RV to make the trip.

"Stick" Season 2 adds great actors like Timothy Olyphant (as Pryce's former golf rival Clark Ross) as regulars and guest stars like recent Emmy winner Rhea Seehorn as Pryce's former coach, with Billy Zane also joining Season 2 in an as-yet-unknown capacity. The first two episodes of the sophomore season dropped on November 4, so catch up before it continues its run.

It's been a strong year for Prime Video, packed with some of the most must-see new and returning shows. From the Alan Ritchson-led fourth season of Reacher and the final season of Eric Kripke's superhero satire series The Boys to Mike Flanagan's latest Stephen King adaptation, Carrie, and the brilliantly underrated Riz Ahmed-led Bait, there's been something for everyone on Prime Video this year. For more recommendations, check out our list of the best shows and movies on Prime Video.

November is already starting strong on Prime Video with a brand-new biopic series about one of the best sports stars to ever live. The Greatest, from executive producer Michael B. Jordan and creator Ben Watkins, stars Jaleen Best as the titular boxing icon, as the highs, lows, and in-betweens of his personal and professional life are chronicled in fine detail.

#3584. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3583. How Big Godzilla Is In Godzilla Minus One Compared To Other Movie Sizes

Godzilla Minus Zero is finally here, and here is how big Godzilla is in the film compared to how tall he is in other Godzilla movies. One of Godzilla's most iconic trademarks is his size, with the terrifying titular titan towering over cities as he brings them to rubble. Tons of iterations of Godzilla have been presented throughout cinema history, with the different Godzillas varying in size, so here is how big the monster is in Godzilla Minus One.

Godzilla Minus Zero is the latest film in the iconic monster movie franchise, and it's once again receiving some incredibly positive reviews, after it followed up the Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One. The last film broke all kinds of box office records, with it being a smash hit and even becoming the largest domestic debut for a live-action Japanese film ever, and Minus Zero looks set to have a similar launch as well. Godzilla Minus Zero's success, combined with its beloved predecessor, has drawn a lot of eyes to the film, with many wondering how big Godzilla is in the latest film, especially when compared with other iterations of the character.

Godzilla is described as being 164 feet (50 meters) in Godzilla Minus One and its newly released sequel, Godzilla Minus Zero, setting the monster at a pretty fearsome size. While 164 feet is far from the biggest that Godzilla has been, this size makes him easily big enough to tower over cities and step on humans without even realizing it. Although some buildings are bigger than Godzilla in the film, the radioactive monster doesn't have much trouble leveling Japan thanks to his size. It's partially because of his size and power that he is recruited to help fight the dangerous King Ghidorah in Minus Zero.

While Godzilla is 164 feet for most of Godzilla Minus One and Minus Zero, this isn't his only size. In fact, Godzilla actually changes size throughout the film. Before being mutated, Godzilla was still a pretty big monster, with him being about 50 feet tall. However, the 164-foot tall version is almost three times as big as it used to be, making Godzilla a horrifying threat.

Godzilla is comparatively small in Godzilla Minus One and Minus Zero when looking at how big he is in other movies, but there is a reason why. Godzilla Minus One and its sequel hearken back to the original Godzilla movie from 1954, and in an attempt to link the two movies, the new movies actually made Godzilla the exact same height as he was in the 1954 original.

Godzilla Minus One and Godzilla Minus Zero sets its titular monster at 164 feet, causing many to wonder how that compares to Godzilla's size in other movies. As it turns out, Godzilla was also 164 feet (50 meters) in the original 1954 film, with Godzilla Minus One remaining consistent with the original movie. Godzilla stayed at this size through 1975's Terror of Mechagodzilla, with Godzilla growing to 262 feet tall for 1984's Return of Godzilla, only for him to grow to a whopping 328 feet in 1991's Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah, the biggest seen in a Japanese Godzilla until Shin Godzilla, in which he was 388 feet.

The first American Godzilla remake was released in 1998, with it portraying Godzilla as 229 feet tall. Godzilla grew even bigger in Legendary's Monsterverse, with him being 354 feet in 2014's Godzilla and growing to 394 feet for Godzilla: King of the Monsters and Godzilla vs. Kong. This makes the Monsterverse's iteration of Godzilla much bigger than the one seen in Godzilla Minus One, but that doesn't mean that they are scarier.

Although Godzilla is comparatively small in Godzilla Minus One and Minus Zero, the ending of the latter film sets the monster up to be even bigger in a potential sequel. As the film demonstrates, Godzilla has intense regenerative abilities, so much so that the heroes of the story claim with confidence that he would survive a nuclear blast. And, once again, it's for this very reason that they recruit Godzilla to fight against King Ghidorah.

Godzilla was injured when fighting the latter, so these regenerative abilities could end up causing Godzilla to grow even bigger upon his return in a sequel to Godzilla Minus Zero, meaning he could potentially grow to a size comparable with some other iterations of the character.

#3582. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3581. James Gray on His ‘Only Real Beef with Streaming’ and the ‘Recurring Nightmare’ That Started at Cannes in 2009

James Gray time-travels back to his Queens roots once again for his latest film, “Paper Tiger.” It’s a location, an atmosphere, a state of mind he’s explored across decades and genres, dating back to his 1994 debut feature, “Little Odessa.” Like “Paper Tiger,” “Little Odessa” also featured the shadows of the Russian mafia looming over a family unit — to devastating ends. But even 30-plus years later, with his new movie — starring Miles Teller, Adam Driver, and Scarlett Johansson — Gray wanted to go just as dangerous.

Adam Driver, for one, has danger in him, according to Gray, who cast the Oscar nominee as a former police officer who links up with the red mafia in the 1980s. Gray recently joined IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio for a wide-ranging, amusingly discursive live conversation at the Virginia Film Festival. One that showcased his knack for impressions — from Luca Guadagnino beckoning Gray out of this year’s Cannes to sit down for the Italian filmmaker’s Bernardo Bertolucci documentary, to the waves of disappointment cresting through Maximilian Schell during an early Venice screening of “Little Odessa.” Related Stories ‘I Play Rocky’ Celebrates Sylvester Stallone the Screenwriter — but Rocky Balboa Was Only the Beginning Inside ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’: How an R Rating, Filming in IMAX, and Epic Kaiju Battles Broke Franchise Tradition

“Almost all great performances have to have some measure of danger in them,” Gray said. “I can actually only think of one that doesn’t have any, which would probably be Jeff Bridges as The Dude in ‘The Big Lebowski,’ which has no danger at all.” (Though John Goodman’s PTSD-addled Vietnam vet in the Coens’ 1998 hardboiled slacker comedy qualifies as dangerous.)

“Adam is a fantastic, intense presence in [‘Paper Tiger’],” said Gray, who wrote “Paper Tiger” with Driver in mind.

Gray also spoke about the “recurring nightmares” for any filmmaker: “You screen your movie, and everybody walks out midway through. I’ve never had that happen to me, thank God.”

But one personal experience of watching this happen to someone else became seared in his unconscious: “When I was on the jury in Cannes [in 2009] … there was a movie made by a fantastic director. I won’t say his name, but he’s a great director of real reputation. And you have to sit in this jury box, which is sort of in the back of a theater, and the seats … when a person gets up, it’s spring-activated, and so it makes this very loud tack. I’m on the jury, and I’m watching this movie, and I start hearing tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack. And people start walking out in droves. And the movie ended, and it was about half full, and people were booing. And that did become a nightmare for me. And by the way, I’m not the only director for whom that’s a nightmare. I’ve talked to many director friends of mine, and they’re like, ‘Oh, yeah. No, I’ve had that dream.'”

James Gray served on the Cannes jury in 2009 under president Isabelle Huppert — whom he reiterated, as Huppert previously did with IndieWire, he has no feud with despite rumors of a fractious deliberation — with such films as Gaspar Noé’s “Enter the Void” and Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist” in the competition. (But again, he’s not naming names here.)

“I know there’s directors who go, ‘I like it. I like when they boo,’ but that’s such a crock,” said Gray. We also asked for his thoughts on audiences dozing off in movies — which some directors, like Lucrecia Martel, have likened to falling asleep in the sun, a reflex of comfort — which certainly happens with some frequency at Cannes as any attendee knows.

“Who likes when you fall asleep during a movie? No, I’m sorry. The movie is required to keep you awake, and as Hitchcock once said, it has to be just long enough to accommodate your bladder’s capacity,” Gray said. “Which, by the way, you know when people say, ‘Oh, well, what do you think of the streaming thing and all that?’ I have only one real beef with streaming, and that’s the pause button, because it is my job to keep you there for an hour and a half, two hours, maybe even three. Where you’re not falling asleep, where you are riveted, where you’re not moving.”

He added, “I can’t stand the people who go, ‘I watched the first half on Tuesday, but I’m gonna catch the second half on a Saturday.’ … There’s nothing you can do about it, and it’s not, it’s not streamer-centered, because most people watch your films now at home. And whether it’s Netflix or Peacock or whatever, it doesn’t matter. The pause button is a problem.”

He pointed to his early relationship to “Vertigo,” a Hitchcock film he didn’t like in the first half, as an example of the virtues of experiencing a movie entirely in one sitting. “The result is so much more rewarding when you are forced to experience the whole thing because it’s like a dream, and you can’t pause your dream. And sometimes you don’t like your dream … sometimes the only way you can get yourself out of that dream is to convince yourself it is a dream in your dream. REM sleep is an hour and a half to two hours a night. What’s a movie’s runtime? It’s about the same thing. It didn’t happen by accident,” Gray said.

#3579. 10 Essential GBA Games Still Disappointingly Missing From Nintendo Switch Online

When the original Game Boy came out, games like the ones people enjoyed on their NES were finally playable on the go, and players loved Nintendo for it. The green and black color palette was a bit of a bummer, but finally was rectified with the Game Boy Color. Even so, most of the games were still pretty basic. The next step was to make a handheld unit that could replicate the superior experience offered on the Super Nintendo, and the Game Boy Advance did precisely that.

Happily, many of the best games from the Game Boy Advance are available to enjoy today with a subscription to Switch Online with the Expansion Pack. However, there are still some absolute gems missing from that library. Here are 10 essential GBA games that belong on Switch Online.

The WarioWare franchise got its start on the Game Boy Advance, with 2003’s WarioWare, Inc.: Mega Microgame$! Until that point, Wario had mostly lived life as a villainous foil to Mario, but then he became an entrepreneur fascinated with the commercial potential for tiny little video games. Or so goes the lore. WarioWare: Twisted! was the second and final entry for the series on the GBA, offering another selection of “microgames” for players to conquer. This time around, the focus was on twisting the Game Boy unit around (hence the title) instead of pressing buttons on the d-pad. Perhaps that’s why the game hasn’t arrived on Switch Online, despite being a critical darling upon release. But it seems like there ought to be some way to make it happen, even so.

Tales of Phantasia, the first game in the long-running Tales series of RPGs, made its debut in Japan on the Super Nintendo in 1995. Like numerous entries in the franchise, it was never released overseas on its original hardware. However, a Game Boy Advance port followed a little over a decade later. Published by Nintendo in 2006, it finally gave players outside Japan the chance to see what we’d been missing: an action-RPG with beautiful visuals. Namco also made slight tweaks to improve the experience, including a reduction in the enemy encounter rate. English voiceover work also was added in North America and Europe. Two decades later, with the Tales series still going, it feels like the right time to bring the first entry to a new audience.

Game Freak has worked on games besides Pokémon for years, and Drill Dozer is one of the developer’s early successes. Known as Screw Breaker in Japan, the platformer presented colorful stages that stood apart from other games in the genre and featured a young girl driving a powerful little tank. A rumble pack built into the cartridge let players feel as if they were dealing actual destruction in the stages they cleared. Unfortunately, the timing for Drill Dozer’s launch wasn’t ideal. Nintendo was already in the middle of a big push to make its DS hardware a success, and didn’t do a lot of marketing for its final releases on older hardware.

Kirby: Nightmare in Dreamland is a remake of Kirby’s Adventure on the NES, but with better visuals and multiplayer action for up to four players, along with new minigames. It also includes some balance adjustments, including more difficult boss encounters and more obvious entrances to hidden areas. There’s not a whole lot to it, but what’s there is perfect for younger players on the hunt for good times with their favorite pink puffball. It would make an excellent addition to the Switch Online library, which already has the more advanced Kirby & The Amazing Mirror. Maybe it can happen around the time Kirby and the World Beyond arrives in 2027.

Lufia is suddenly alive again, with Lufia 1 and 2 getting remakes in 2027. While the announcement that those beloved titles are on their way was most welcome, there has been no word on the later installments. Lufia: The Ruins of Lore, which launched on the Game Boy Advance, would be a natural addition to the Switch Online library. It’s a side story that takes place 20 years after the events depicted in Lufia 2: Rise of the Sinistrals. Combat is turn-based, but battles are triggered only when the player encounters visible enemies on the map. It’s also possible to recruit monsters, rather than always killing them, and they grant powerful attacks in battle. If Clear River Games can’t get the rights to localize more entries in the series, perhaps The Ruins of Lore can still make an appearance on Switch Online.

Super Puzzle Fighter 2 Turbo debuted in arcades in 1996, and came home later that year for the PlayStation and Saturn. It features chibi versions of popular characters from Street Fighter 2, who are duking it out by matching falling blocks in a puzzle game. As colorful stones fall from the top of the screen, they fuse to form larger blocks. Clearing them sets off dazzling combo chains, which is a dopamine hit that’s hard to resist. It’s all too easy to spend hours playing the simple little puzzle game, even if you don’t know Chun-Li from Felicia. Fans of the fighting series will find even more to like in the background and character design. It translates just beautifully to the Game Boy Advance, even without “Turbo” in the title. The opportunity to battle friends online today would be at least as welcome as the link cable option was back in the day. If you’re not ready to wait, you can also find it included as part of the Capcom Fighting Collection.

Pinball might not be the first thing that comes to mind when you think of Pokémon, but it worked perfectly in Pokémon Pinball: Ruby & Sapphire. Developed by Jupiter Corporation, which is best known these days for its picross games, the action pinball title offers two unique tables. Mostly, it plays like standard pinball with Pokémon fixings. Visuals are bright and cheery, and unique modes give players new goals (such as hitting a Pokémon several times before a timer expires and it vanishes). New Pokémon releases and spinoffs happen fairly regularly, so it seems likely that we’ll get the chance to play Pokémon Pinball: Ruby & Sapphire again sooner or later. If we get our way, it’ll be the former.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Players are busy talking about Onimusha: Way of the Sword these days, as the series enjoys a proper revival after more than a decade with no new entries. The franchise dates back to Onimusha: Warlords on the PlayStation 2 in 2001. Following that popular release, the series remained highly active for several years. Along the way, Onimusha Tactics arrived on the Game Boy Advance, presenting a dark side story that was at odds with its cheerier visuals. Combat is no longer action-based. Instead, player characters occupy a Fire Emblem-esque grid, where they work to overcome the opposing force so the plot can advance. It’s a strategy game for genre newcomers, and right now would be the perfect time to revive it for a new audience.

Capcom has produced numerous compilations of Mega Man games, but Mega Man & Bass remains relatively elusive, despite being better than some of the mainline entries. Originally released on the Super Famicom as RockMan & Forte in 1998, the action platformer wasn’t released in North America with its new name for another five years. When it did finally arrive, it did so as a Game Boy Advance port. It offered more challenging stages than Mega Man fans were accustomed to, with the tougher Mega Man 9 still a few years away. The game’s big hook was that it let players enjoy the adventure either as Mega Man or as Bass, his more agile rival. The robots play differently, which means the robot stages offer new challenges even after a player has cleared the game once. Considering the title’s absence from recent compilations, a Switch Online appearance would make perfect sense and fill in a vital gap.

Before Square acquired Quest in 2002, the team produced several games in its Ogre Battle franchise, starting with Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen in 1993. The final installment was Tactics Ogre: The Knight of Lodis, a tactical RPG that serves as a prequel to the overall series. It follows Alphonse Loeher, a Lodis soldier who turns against his former allies while battling to defend the kingdom of Ovis. Combat plays out on expansive maps that feature varying elevation and terrain, much as in a subsequent project from the team, Final Fantasy Tactics Advance. Despite the handheld format, the game offered a compelling adventure for serious fans of strategy games, with numerous classes and weapons that made combat varied and difficult. The game has been unavailable for a quarter-century and would make a fine addition to the Switch Online library, especially if Square Enix has no plans for a remake along the lines of Tactics Ogre: Reborn.

#3578. ‘What Happened to Nina?’ Author’s #1 Bestseller Officially Heads to TV

The streaming era has paved the way for a much wider selection of books to reach the screen, whether as films or television series. Netflix, in particular, has been aggressive in snatching up the rights to acclaimed and bestselling novels, finding success this year with everything from Shelby Van Pelt's Remarkably Bright Creatures to Alice Feeney's His & Hers. Now, it's officially Australian thriller author Dervla McTiernan's time to shine once again. Her star has been on the rise for a while now, with two of her previous novels, The Murder Rule and the acclaimed What Happened to Nina?, both being optioned for adaptation by FX and Lingo Pictures, respectively. Yet another of her titles is now about to get the television treatment.

Easy Tiger Productions, the banner behind the acclaimed romantic comedy series Colin From Accounts, has won a heated bidding war for the rights to McTiernan's 2026 novel Three Reasons for Revenge. At this time, a streamer or other distributor has not been set, meaning it'll still have to be taken out to the wider market and sold before it can really hit the ground running. It does, however, already have a big name on board to write in Shaun Grant. Best known of late for penning the Jacob Elordi-led miniseries The Narrow Road to the Deep North and the 2021 Caleb Landry Jones-led psychological drama Nitram, he shared in a statement how confident he was from the beginning that McTiernan's latest was destined for the small screen. "From the moment I first read Three Reasons for Revenge, I immediately envisaged it as a television series,” he said. “It is a supremely crafted thriller full of surprises, and I thank Dervla for entrusting Easy Tiger and myself with her creation.”

Three Reasons for Revenge revolves around "three seemingly unconnected people caught in a lethal web of deceit and unhealed wounds." All three live in completely different houses throughout Melbourne, yet they all receive similarly mysterious gifts, each of which is painstakingly tailored to fit its recipient to a T. However, they're all carefully thought out to destroy their lives from the inside. It's left up to Detective Sergeant Judith Lee to unravel who could've had such intimate knowledge of each of the three people's lives and vulnerabilities to craft such monstrous presents. Making things more curious is that they all seem to tie back to the sudden and mysterious disappearance of a woman who had reported an assault less than a day before she vanished.

Following its launch earlier this year, McTiernan's latest soared to the top of Australian bestseller charts across all genres, giving the author, with over 1 million copies sold, another big winner. Easy Tiger made sense, then, as the perfect partner for the project given their status as Australia's biggest production company. In addition to Colin From Accounts, which wrapped up with Season 3 earlier this year, they also backed Netflix's neo-western series Territory, Disney's 2013 film Saving Mr. Banks, and the Australian legal thriller The Twelve, starring the late Sam Neill. In his own statement, Easy Tiger's CEO Rob Gibson hailed the collaboration with both McTiernan and Grant as a match made in heaven.

"There’s no doubt Dervla’s highly entertaining book will find a place not only on your shelves but on your TV screen. Dervla is a master at creating a gripping thriller plot, and Shaun is the perfect writer to adapt her book. We’re so delighted to be working with them both.”

Stay tuned here at Collider for more updates on the Three Reasons for Revenge adaptation as it seeks a home.

#3577. Emily Feingold Hired as EVP, Communications for The Walt Disney Company

Emily Feingold has been named Executive Vice President, Communications for The Walt Disney Company. She will begin her job next Monday.

Feingold is a veteran executive and is widely respected by the press as a straight shooter. She joins Disney after nearly nine years at Netflix, where she rose to become Vice President and Head of Communications for the U.S. and Canada. At the streaming giant, Feingold worked on corporate, financial, product and technology, advertising, content, marketing and consumer products communications. She advised senior leadership through some of Netflix’s biggest moments, including when co-founder Reed Hastings was succeeded as CEO by Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters. She also was in place when Netflix moved into advertising, live events, and gaming, as well as during its failed bid for Warner Bros. Discovery. Related Stories James Gray on His ‘Only Real Beef with Streaming’ and the ‘Recurring Nightmare’ That Started at Cannes in 2009 ‘I Play Rocky’ Celebrates Sylvester Stallone the Screenwriter — but Rocky Balboa Was Only the Beginning

Before Netflix, Feingold was Senior Vice President of Corporate Strategy and Communications at Andell Inc., a private investment firm, and Vice President of Corporate Communications at Ralph Lauren. She began her career at the White House.

At Disney, Feingold will report to Paul Roeder, Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Communications Officer, and oversee media relations, enterprise editorial, and executive, brand, financial and technology communications.

“Emily is one of the best in the business,” said Roeder. “She combines sharp instincts, broad experience and the trust and respect of colleagues and journalists alike. She’s led communications through some of the most transformative moments in our industry, and she’ll be a tremendous asset as we head into an exciting chapter for Disney.”Feingold succeeds David Jefferson, Executive Vice President, Communications, who has accepted the company’s voluntary early retirement offer after 15 years with Disney. Jefferson is a former journalist who spent two decades reporting and editing for The Wall Street Journal and Newsweek. He will remain through the end of the month.

“David has been a trusted voice and steady hand for Disney through some of the most consequential moments in our history,” said Roeder. “I’ve known him since his days as a reporter, and I’m deeply grateful for his counsel, his friendship and everything he’s done for this company. I wish him every success in what comes next.”
