#3576. X-Men Debuts Hardcore New Sentinel Design

The X-Men meet Marvel's latest Sentinel, which is way scarier and possibly more dangerous than the original design. The towering Sentinels are the physical manifestation of human hatred against mutants in the Marvel Universe, manufactured by ordinary human beings and engineered to hunt and execute individuals purely based on their genes. Their unfeeling programming strips away any possibility of empathy, and since they're mass-produced on assembly lines, the X-Men can never be fully certain that they have destroyed the very last of the robots. Like Ultron, there will always be at least one Sentinel out there restarting the cycle.

Throughout X-Men history, these automated hunter-killers have launched devastating campaigns against mutantkind, leading mutants to the brink of extinction on multiple occasions. The most catastrophic assault takes place during E Is for Extinction, where a fleet of wild Mega-Sentinels ambush the island nation of Genosha and slaughter over sixteen million mutant citizens in a matter of minutes. In the dark future timelines of Days of Future Past, advanced Hound-directed Sentinels successfully hunt down and execute nearly every superhero and mutant on Earth. Although the X-Men's joint efforts allow them to slice through single Sentinels, the army of robots never ends.

As House of X perfectly explained, "artificial intelligence is like fire. it's a discovery, not an invention." As much as the X-Men may try to get rid of the Sentinels, the robotic villains will only come back stronger and with new weapons to fulfill their objectives.

As Sarah Gaunt and her group of Wolverine-like Scavengers prepare to become the X-Men's evil counterparts, the Uncanny X-Men's fabulous Dazzler, Rogue, and Monet St. Croix return to Greymalkin Prison, where they come face to face with an experimental Sentinel. Sporting two extra arms and a permanently open mouth, this prototype Sentinel activates its lethal mode to eliminate the mutant heroes, shooting them with lasers and attempting to crush them like flies with its enlarged hands. The experimental Sentinel's additional limbs allow it to fight multiple mutants at a time, even without using its legs.

Luckily for the heroes, the prototype Sentinel picked the worst possible opponents. Although Dazzler is left with little to use against the giant robot, Rogue easily destroys one of its hands, and Monet flies straight across its head, killing it for good. The true size of the Sentinel is only evident when the three X-Men stand over its inert body, revealing a particularly intricate but still unfinished design. Had a different, more inexperienced team met this new iteration of Bolivar Trask's invention, they would likely have struggled to contain it much more.

Marvel's new era of X-Men comics has witnessed a terrifying paradigm change in anti-mutant technology that trades the rigid metallic giants of old for grotesque bio-organic horrors. In Gail Simone’s Uncanny X-Men, the Sentinels have branched out into several different visceral nightmares. The Bloodhound Stealth Sentinels are canine-shaped tracking drones with chainsaw-like teeth, while a wave of Sentinel-human hybrids sport pitch-black eyes and flexible slender bodies. Most unsettling of all are the red, gelatinous Organic Sentinels encountered in the Louisiana underworld, which rely on a biological core that grants them rapid cellular regeneration.

Jean Grey isn't the only telepath in Marvel with extraordinary abilities. Meet the seven of Marvel's strongest telepaths who could rival her power.

At the moment, these nightmarish new Sentinels are more of an agonizing nuisance rather than the X-Men's primary threats. Powerhouses like Rogue and Monet can come in and destroy them in between their battles with the likes of the sadistic warden Sarah Gaunt and her predatory Scavengers, the demonic Wyvern, and Beast's evil mastermind self from the future, the Chairman. However, as clandestine programs continue to perfect the robots, the Sentinels are only getting more dangerous. It's only a matter of time until they scale up and evolve into an unstoppable threat that the X-Men can no longer keep up with.

#3573. The Johnny Depp Comeback Hits Judgment Day with ‘Ebenezer’: How Paramount Is Carefully Reintroducing the Controversial Star

Hollywood studios turned away Johnny Depp eight years ago. With “Ebenezer,” Paramount Pictures is betting that audiences have not rejected him too. The “A Christmas Carol” adaptation, out November 13, marks a decisive moment for the studio, as it was one of the first films boarded by the company after its 2025 acquisition by Skydance.

Depp got some positive social media attention Monday evening when he was filmed “wyling out” and “wreaking havoc” in the Christmas Market of New York’s Bryant Park — as Scrooge, of course. In his first major pre-release promotional stop for “Ebenezer,” Depp donned a fright wig and make-up to enact some staged bah-humbugging, which included popping balloons, knocking over a Christmas tree, and playfully antagonizing an on-site Santa Claus. The stunt was Depp’s second in-character appearance as Scrooge, coming three months after a similarly interactive appearance at San Diego Comic-Con that also generated mounds of social media content from passerby. Later on at the event, Scrooge appeared onstage during Collider’s Directors on Directing panel to debut the first “Ebenezer” trailer. Related Stories Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money The Bay Theater in Palisades Village, Closed Since the LA Wildfires, Will Reopen Thanks to Paramount and Rick Caruso

The approach leans into how audiences know Depp, who became one of the industry’s biggest stars in the aughts with his quirked-up performances in the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise and various Tim Burton joints. But several publicity veterans note that it’s also a strategy that helps the star skirt addressing himself: a typical component to the modern promotional gauntlet of podcast appearances and junketing. Paramount and representatives for Depp declined to comment for this story.

Indeed, the last time Depp was promoting a blockbuster in character was at Warner Bros.’ San Diego Comic-Con panel in 2018, where he appeared as Gellert Grindelwald, the seductively authoritarian wizard within J.K. Rowling’s world of “Harry Potter,” to promote the second “Fantastic Beasts” prequel. Depp was mired in controversy at the time, as his ex-wife, Amber Heard, alleged that he had been “physically abusive” in court documents filed in their divorce case. Depp denied the claims. Making things more awkward — Heard appeared at the same studio presentation, popping up an hour later for a panel hyping “Aquaman.”

Two years later, Depp departed from a third (and what ended up to be the final) “Fantastic Beasts” entry. On Instagram, the actor posted that he had been “asked to resign” by the studio. Depp had just lost a U.K. libel trial against The Sun, in which a judge ruled that an article reporting that the actor was a “wife beater” was found to be “substantially true.”

But Depp later claimed victory in a U.S. defamation trial against Heard herself. Heard had written a Washington Post op-ed in which she described herself as a survivor of domestic abuse. Depp claimed the article damaged his reputation and career; both parties argued the other was the aggressor through the grueling six-week spectacle. An initial jury ruling sided with Depp on three separate claims of defamation, ordering Heard pay him $10.35 million in damages. Heard won on one of her three counterclaims of defamation, ordering Depp to pay her $2 million. A later appeal by Heard ended with a settlement in which she agreed to pay $1 million to Depp.

The highly-gawked-at and internet-scrutinized trial reignited his fame and infamy, depending on your perspective. Once a big-screen titan, he was now ubiquitous on social media, particularly TikTok, emerging with an ardent online fanbase forged by a conviction that he was a man who had been rashly cast aside during the #MeToo movement’s prominence in the late 2010’s.

With “Ebenezer,” Paramount has the unique assignment of capitalizing on that celebrity, without inviting relitigation of an ugly legal battle that would cloud the sunny promotion of a family feature. Hence, the in-character appearances, along with underlining Depp’s penchant for transformative turns (though no further ones are planned). A promotional video featuring snippets of cast interviews, including the likes of Ian McKellen, Daisy Ridley, and Tramell Tillman, praise the actor as giving “a performance the likes of which you’ve never seen before.”

“A less clever route would be turning the release into a ‘comeback’ victory lap. The result could be an unnecessary and noisy polarization of views, reviving the very controversy the studio would prefer to move beyond,” says media lawyer and crisis manager Amber Melville-Brown, who heads the media and reputation team at the law firm Withers. “A campaign built around vindication invites an argument about who, precisely, has been vindicated and for what — starting the debate over again. A campaign built around the performance sparks a different conversation.”

Meanwhile, Paramount has been careful to show “Ebenezer” to select audiences so far. The film was unveiled Sunday in New York City with a “special screening” at the Whitby Hotel’s 147-seat screening room — an intimate venue for the first unveiling of a studio feature. A handful of press outlets and more influencers were invited to a small carpet. One front-facing video posted by a guest featured her meeting Depp and calling the occasion “my sign from God that I chose the right path today.” A London premiere will take place at Odeon Luxe Leicester Square on Monday.

In another shrewd booking, Depp made a surprise onstage appearance during Aerosmith’s Hollywood Bowl concert on October 29. While other actors may tap in for a late-night spot or “Hot Ones” interview to mark the home stretch of film promotion, Depp instead let a guitar solo on “Train Kept A-Rollin'” do the talking.

Down the line, the “Ebenezer” review embargo will lift November 12, mere hours before public screenings begin — almost always a sign that a studio has little confidence in finding good PR from the critic class. The film’s director, Ti West, has usually drawn positive reviews through his career, mostly known as an indie horror darling until this first studio feature.

But most importantly for Paramount, “Ebenezer” doesn’t need to be a blockbuster to find success. The film’s production budget netted out to a rather modest $38 million, giving it a much easier pathway to theatrical profitability than Depp’s previous mega-budget tentpoles. Along with that comes hopes to leg out through the holiday season and a bank on grosses from overseas territories, where other older male movie stars like Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise have better retained their ability to sell tickets.

Rival studios are looking closely at whether audiences still see Depp as a big screen draw. Lionsgate is already in the Depp business for the revenge thriller “Day Drinker,” releasing in March. And at Disney’s D23 Expo in August, “Pirates of the Caribbean” producer Jerry Bruckheimer floated hopes to get the star on board for a sixth installment. That franchise has laid dormant for nearly a decade, despite numerous reports of development teams tinkering on a Depp-less take. In one of the more interesting quotes from the “Ebenezer” event in New York, Depp spoke with Entertainment Tonight and slid in a dig at the 2017 entry “Dead Men Tell No Tales,” saying he’d be open to a franchise return but noting that “the only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.”

But when Depp was first jettisoned from Hollywood’s A-list, major studios had begun to tire of his antics. There were reports of erratic on-set behavior, sky-high salary demands, and — in the true offender for studios — diminishing box office returns. The “Pirates” films still made money, but Depp headlined several costly bombs, including “Alice Through the Looking Glass” and “Mortdecai,” which had left companies less eager to write big checks, particularly given his public relations scandals.

But Depp’s absence may have not curbed his following. A National Research Group study from earlier this year found that he was the seventh-most cited name by people, especially in Europe, when they wre asked to name five actors or actresses that would motivate them to see “a new movie in a cinema,” even though he’s been away from the big screen for nearly a decade. Over those years, a growing refrain in the business has been that some movie stars have kneecapped their ability to open films by signing on to streaming productions, curbing consumers’ association of them with theaters. In that context, Depp may prove to be a unicorn, having essentially sat out years of the industry chasing Netflix — even if it wasn’t his choice to.

#3571. '9-1-1' Disappoints Fans Again With a Major Eddie Problem in Season 10

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for 9-1-1 Season 10, Episode 4.9-1-1 opened its tenth season with two especially compelling storylines: a volcanic eruption and a Buddie fight. While the volcano emergency was resolved in three episodes, it looked like Buck (Oliver Stark) and Eddie's (Ryan Guzman) argument would go on for longer. On the surface, they were arguing because Eddie had given Buck parental advice that he wasn't ready to hear. The deeper issue at play, though, seemed to be that, once again, Buck and Eddie were having conflict over the more ambiguous and undefined parts of their friendship that the two have not yet been ready to put to words.

The solution here seemed to be a simple one: Buck and Eddie needed to redefine the terms of their dynamic and their places in each other's lives, whatever that may look like, because what they'd had before was no longer enough. Instead, 9-1-1's latest episode, Season 10, Episode 4, "Imposter Syndrome," wraps this argument up way too quickly with an unearned off-screen resolution. While this is disappointing for multiple reasons, it's ultimately a symptom of 9-1-1's biggest problem at the moment: every time the show sets up a substantial storyline for Eddie, it ultimately sidelines him and fails to deliver.

Since returning from Texas at the end of Season 8, Eddie hasn't gotten a proper storyline of his own. Occasionally, 9-1-1 will lean into the fan-favorite pairing of Buck and Eddie, but every Buddie-centric storyline as of late always changes direction to become about Buck. When Buck pointed out last season that Eddie hadn't "even looked at a woman in a year" and pushed him to find someone, it looked like 9-1-1 might focus on Eddie and actually answer this question, potentially by giving him a storyline about his sexuality. Instead, the episode became all about Buck's hookups with a married couple. When the two had a fight and then got into a car accident in "Mother's Boy," the whole episode became about Eddie having to save Buck, and only Buck got to experience lingering effects from this trauma in the coming episodes.

There was no exploration of how the car accident affected Eddie, or the lingering impact that the racism and homophobia directed at him throughout that episode had on him. Even when Eddie got stabbed in the Season 9 finale, he recovered off-screen, and his pain was used to fuel Buck's storyline of choosing to foster Theo. Season 10's Buck and Eddie fight was set up to focus on Buck and Eddie's dynamic, but it could have also explored their own separate parenting issues. Instead, in "Imposter Syndrome," the storyline becomes all about Buck having problems with Theo (Lincoln and Theodore Sykes), because he still refuses to even try to parent him. Eddie is sidelined the whole episode, and he and Buck make up mostly off-screen, ending their argument with a brief conversation where Eddie has to comfort a self-deprecating Buck instead of having his own feelings acknowledged.

Eddie Diaz is one of the most captivating characters on television right now. He has a deeply compelling backstory, a fierce love for the people in his life, and an unshakable belief, on a fundamental level, that he doesn't deserve good things. There is so much for 9-1-1 to explore when it comes to Eddie's character, from his grief over recently losing Bobby and his abuela (Ana Mercedes), to his complicated relationship with religion, to why dating has never come easily to him. He hasn't had a proper storyline with Christopher (Gavin McHugh) since either of them moved back to Los Angeles, and the show hasn't given any focus to how Eddie felt about having stepped in for Chimney (Kenneth Choi) to primarily serve as a paramedic alongside Hen (Aisha Hinds) over a season ago.

The Buddie dynamic is certainly an important one, but Buck and Eddie have not been given the same treatment by the narrative, and every one of their shared storylines now always becomes about Buck. 9-1-1 needs to start focusing on Eddie's side of these storylines as well, but he also needs to get some deeper storylines of his own. Eddie already doesn't get enough to do, but when he does, 9-1-1 does not linger on him long enough to explore his feelings and the deeper implications that these storylines have had on him. In its tenth season, 9-1-1 is still underutilizing one of its best characters, and it needs to finally do right by him.

9-1-1 airs Thursdays at 8:00 P.M. EST on ABC.

#3570. The 8 Best Castlevania Games Of All Time, Ranked

Castlevania is one of the most beloved franchises in video game history, despite a period of 13 years when we didn’t see a new installment until the launch of Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse earlier this year.

Over the years, the games have provided a variety of experiences, mixed with rich lore built on the vampire myth. With so many games available to choose from, it can be difficult to know where to begin if you haven’t touched the series in a while. Accordingly, here is our ranked list of the 8 best Castlevania games. It should make an excellent starting point.

When Castlevania came to the Super Nintendo, it needed to impress players who were still deciding whether they wanted to spend money on a new generation of Nintendo hardware. Fortunately for everyone involved, the team at Konami was up to the task. Super Castlevania 4 features beautiful environments, as well as a hero who can now whip in eight directions, even while jumping. It’s also possible to grapple to distant points, or to wield the whip as a shield. Early use of Mode 7 rotation provided some visual showpieces to go along with parallax depth that brought static environments to life. The adventure starts outside the castle, allowing Simon to explore its harsh exterior before venturing inside for a final showdown with the lord of the manor. If you’re looking for a starting point, you could do much worse, and it’s conveniently available as part of the Castlevania Anniversary Collection on Switch, PlayStation 4, PC, and Xbox One.

The Super Nintendo wasn’t the only hardware to feature a high-quality Castlevania game during the 16-bit era. Castlevania: Bloodlines took a unique approach, introducing a hero who strikes with a spear. He can use it to access alternate routes that the other character (who fights with a more traditional whip) cannot. The pacing was fast and furious, in keeping with many Genesis games of that time. The setting was also more modern than the other classic titles, taking place during the first World War. Stages are inspired by locations around the globe, including a visit to the Leaning Tower of Pisa, among other attractions. Throw in some stunning visual tricks that made full use of the Genesis hardware, along with a beautiful score from composer Michiru Yamane (who would go on to compose for Symphony of the Night) and you have a truly special entry in the franchise.

Originally developed for the Sharp X68000 and released on that hardware as Akumajo Dracula, Castlevania Chronicles was one of the final Castlevania games built in the classical style. It actually is a remake of 1986’s first entry in the series. 1993’s version offered greatly improved visuals and sound, while providing generally fair but challenging gameplay that is some of the most difficult the series ever offered. Some new twists maintain the element of surprise, even as players retread familiar ground, but there’s no better way to experience the original adventure, as its developers intended. When I checked earlier this year, the digital version of the prettied up PlayStation port was still available to purchase through the PlayStation Store on a PlayStation 3 console, if you add the funds to your wallet on newer hardware. Or you can hunt down a physical copy of that port, which should play just fine on your PlayStation 3.

If more people had easily been able to play the game as its developers intended, Castlevania: Rondo of Blood might be remembered today as the premier Castlevania experience. Sadly, the game remained exclusive to the PC Engine CD hardware for a long time. It didn’t head to North America and Europe until it arrived on PSP as part of 2007’s Castlevania: The Dracula X Chronicles collection, and as a Virtual Console selection in 2010, almost a decade and a half after its initial release. The closest we got in the meantime was Dracula X on the Super Nintendo. That title was a mostly unsuccessful attempt to compress Rondo of Blood’s essence to fit on a cartridge — and to reach hardware that hadn’t bombed outside of Japan. The same plot and characters returned, as did many enemy sprites. Both games began in a town on fire. However, the branching stages were absent, replaced by abbreviated challenges that players found frustrating. Some characters from the original version weren’t even playable, and the sound quality suffered immensely. Rondo of Blood is an important game in Castlevania’s timeline, and concludes with the events that serve as a prologue to Symphony of the Night. If you haven’t yet done so, you should play through it soon.

Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow followed one year after Harmony of Dissonance, which in some respects was the more spectacular of the pair. But despite its inferior visuals, Aria of Sorrow offered the richer experience on a mechanical level. Players control Soma Cruz, who blacks out during the first solar eclipse of the century and awakens in Dracula’s castle. There, he finds he can absorb the essence of the monsters he vanquishes, a useful way to gain the strength he’ll need to reach Dracula’s throne room and rescue his classmate. The adventure is surprisingly complex, given the tiny hardware that houses it, and still a lot of fun to play. You can most easily experience it and other games of that era as part of Castlevania Advance Collection on Switch, PlayStation 4, PC, and Xbox One.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The 8-bit era established Castlevania as a force to be reckoned with, ensuring it survived long enough to continue breaking new ground over the decades. But those early titles aren’t always a lot of fun to play today. The original game sometimes felt cheap and rather bland, even near release. Its sequel had an interesting plot and ambitious new mechanics, but it confounded many players with unclear, non-linear objectives. Then Castlevania 3: Dracula’s Curse came around and perfected the formula, providing multiple heroes with lore (which Netflix later explored with an animated series) and unique play styles, along with diverging paths through gorgeous stages that pushed the NES hardware harder than ever before. It’s the finest single example of what Castlevania could be during that era, and well worth revisiting today.

Check our full Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review for all the details, but the short version is this: you need to play the game. It respects the series’ history while mapping out a potential future we hope the developers will one day realize with follow-up titles. The 2.5D visuals give each area a new sense of depth, while enabling the satisfying Metroidvania mechanics players have enjoyed since Symphony of the Night changed the franchise forever. Fluid movement during combat, a killer soundtrack to match the moonlit ambience of the visuals, and a brave new hero all add up to one of the very finest entries the series has ever seen.

Nearly 30 years after its release, there’s still no topping Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. It’s the game credited with taking Metroid’s design and fusing it with the gothic adventuring players associate with the Castlevania series. The sprawling castle was populated by nightmarish creatures, many of them familiar and many of them not. Stripped of his powerful weapons, Alucard explores the castle and seeks to put down his fearsome father once and for all. But as players learned, there’s much more to the adventure than the simple castle they glimpse beneath the moonlight. One of the happiest surprises in video games came when players looked at things through a new perspective, thanks to some holy spectacles. The shift in focus opened up an unfamiliar pathway, revealing that they weren’t even halfway done with their adventure. It was the game that kept on giving, and it still hasn’t stopped.

#3569. X-Men’s First-Ever Live-Action Mister Sinister Actor Breaks Silence On MCU Debut

The Marvel Cinematic Universe's X-Men reboot features a lineup of fresh new faces, but one particular star isn't entirely new to Marvel Studios.

In an interview on Jimmy Kimmel Live, Adam Driver revealed some surprising information about his relationship with Marvel. The Academy Award nominee is set to portray Nathaniel Milbury, better known as the villain Mister Sinister, in the highly anticipated X-Men reboot. Directed by Jake Schreier, the movie will introduce a new generation of mutants to the MCU, with Driver joining a massive ensemble cast that includes several rising stars.

Driver revealed how he has been offered roles by Marvel Studios before. However, up until now, he has declined all of them. During the discussion, the actor explained why he finally decided to join the Marvel Universe after years of unsuccessful recruitment efforts. According to Driver, his longtime appreciation for the X-Men characters played a major role in his decision.

Driver told the late-night host that growing up as a fan of the superhero mutant team and pretending to be Wolverine while playing with his cousin who took on the part of Sabretooth. As a result, these childhood memories played a significant role in why he was more inclined to say yes when he was offered the role of Mister Sinister.

Although Driver spent years rejecting MCU roles, he made it clear that he genuinely likes Marvel's franchises. He further elaborated, saying that the timing and circumstances surrounding the X-Men reboot made the project more appealing for him. The actor added that Schreier's creative direction convinced him to finally enter the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

Despite his enthusiasm, Driver admitted that joining such a recognizable franchise comes with a lot of pressure. The actor said that the film would attract a massive audience, meaning any shortcomings in his performance could be picked apart by fans who loved his villainous character. However, the actor assured viewers that, as someone who loved X-Men growing up, he intends to do justice to both the property and the supervillain.

Driver's character, Mister Sinister, is one of the X-Men's most infamous villains in Marvel Comics. Known for being a scientist who is obsessed with genetics, the character has frequently conducted experiments involving mutants and their abilities. Created by Chris Claremont, Mister Sinister was first mentioned in Uncanny X-Men #212 in 1986, appeared as a silhouette in the following issue, and made his full debut in The Uncanny X-Men #221 in 1987.

#3568. Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52

Sebastián Lelio, the humanistic Chilean filmmaker whose trans drama “A Fantastic Woman” won the Best International Feature Film Oscar in 2018, has died at age 52.

The Chilean publication Emol first revealed the news that he was found dead in his home in Santiago on Friday, November 6, amid an undisclosed health issue. His body was discovered by his partner, the actress/director Amalia Kassai, who starred in his final film, the protest musical “The Wave” from Cannes 2025. Kassai also posted a statement in Spanish on her Instagram account.

Lelio was reportedly mid-production on the feature “Chilean Poet,” adapted from Alejandro Zambra’s Viking-published 2022 novel. Along with “A Fantastic Woman,” he also directed the Hasidic lesbian romance “Disobedience” in the same year, 2017; it starred Rachel McAdams and Rachel Weisz, and helped bring the filmmaker to international prominence. In 2013, he directed Paulina García to a Berlinale Silver Bear Best Actress win with “Gloria,” a late-in-life romantic comedy about a 58-year-old divorcee starting over again. He remade his own film in 2018 in English as “Gloria Bell,” released by A24 and starring Julianne Moore in the role García originated, opposite John Turturro.

Lelio regularly collaborated with the Chilean brothers Pablo Larraín and Juan de Dios Larraín, who served as producers on nearly all of his films. They were also collaborating with Lelio on his ongoing, now-final feature. Born in Argentina, he emigrated to Chile at age two with his mother and later graduated from Chilean Film School, after which he launched his career with short films and music videos. His debut narrative feature, “The Sacred Family,” premiered at the San Sebastián International Film Festival in Spain before his follow-up, “Navidad,” premiered at Cannes in 2009. The post-Chilean-earthquake drama “The Year of the Tiger,” starring beloved Chilean actor Luis Dubó, debuted at Locarno in 2011.

His fourth feature, “Gloria,” shot digitally and with a script and dialogue developed in part with his actors, including García, received U.S. distribution from Roadside Attractions and was widely regarded as one of the best films of 2013.

Lelio directed the first Best International Feature Oscar entry to win the Academy Award with 2017’s Golden Bear-nominated “A Fantastic Woman,” an exuberantly styled drama that put trans actress Daniela Vega on the international map. As Vega consulted on the script, it’s widely seen as a groundbreaker of trans portrayals onscreen in the 21st century. And it helped reform the perception and attitudes toward transness in Lelio and Vega’s home of Chile — and inevitably, within the Academy.

Lelio’s favorite films on the 2022 Sight & Sound poll included “La Dolce Vita,” “Playtime,” “The 400 Blows,” and “Singin’ in the Rain,” and you can feel their impact across his often irreverent, at times burstingly colorful, playful body of work.

His 2017 TIFF premiere “Disobedience” received U.S. distribution from Bleecker Street, and told the story of a forbidden, transgressive romance between two Orthodox Jewish women (McAdams and Weisz) in North London. The tender, taboo drama performed well in North America, grossing nearly $3.5 million domestic during a spring-through-summer 2018 run.

Lelio, that year, deftly remade “Gloria” as “Gloria Bell” with Julianne Moore as the free-spirited divorcee being wooed by John Turturro, and weighing choices in her next chapter living as a yoga instructor in Los Angeles. Returning to filming after the pandemic, Lelio broadened his collaborative scope to adapt “Room” author Emma Donoghue’s “The Wonder,” with Donoghue and Alice Birch co-writing the script with him. Florence Pugh starred as a British nurse sent to Ireland to observe a miraculous “fasting girl,” in a film that played Telluride and streamed on Netflix to strong reviews.

His last film, “The Wave,” took a minute to get off the ground after playing out of competition in Cannes 2025. The story of an introverted music student whose passion for protest is awakened amid a growing feminist movement on campus, “The Wave” received a small release from Wolfe Video earlier this year and received positive response throughout its festival run.

The status of Lelio’s final film isn’t known right now, but we can imagine that Lelio’s sensitive approach to character — and unstable identities finding their footing, their purest expression — will carry into the new work. The Larraín brothers were also producing the film, with Lelio’s regular cinematographer Benjamín Echazarreta on board as DP.

#3567. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3566. Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

It does not take long for the new trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” to invoke the most discourse-inducing scene from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” In fact, the very first words we hear are “You heard the story about Bruce Lee getting his ass kicked by a stuntman?” Another reference to the Bruce Lee scene follows soon after, long before we hear any mention of Rick Dalton or any of the more consequential events of the first film..

The Netflix pseudo-sequel, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino, sees Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role as Cliff Booth. It’s billed as a separate adventure that happens to feature one of the film’s main characters — Leonardo DiCaprio is either completely absent or an incredibly well-kept secret, and Tarantino has said the film shares more DNA with Elmore Leonard’s paperback crime novels than the hangout movie style that defined the first film. But the marketing had to remind audiences who Cliff Booth is, and it’s curious that the second trailer’s primary reference point is a scene that is more memorable for the controversies it sparked than its role in the film’s plot. No mention is made, for instance, of the part Cliff played in dispatching several members of the Manson Family. Related Stories Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52 Emily Feingold Hired as EVP, Communications for The Walt Disney Company

A brief recap for those lucky enough to have been offline during the original saga. “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” features a scene in which Cliff is left to hang around a TV set while DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton shoots an episode. While killing time, he ends up in a fight with Bruce Lee (played by Mike Moh). Neither man is particularly polite to the other, with Cliff appearing more interested in Lee’s sidekick role on “The Green Hornet” than his higher profile movie roles, and Lee quickly challenges him to a fight. Each man wins one round of the fight before it’s broken up, ensuring there’s no clear winner — but the mere fact that Cliff was able to throw a martial arts legend into the side of a car is a feather in his cap.

Following the film’s release, Bruce Lee’s daughter Shannon publicly objected to the way the film portrayed her father.

“It’s unfortunate because it has started this narrative in some places where some people are saying, ‘Oh, Bruce Lee was an asshole,’” Shannon Lee said in 2020. “Look, everybody can be an asshole sometimes. I can be arrogant and angry in my life — is that something I would say I am like generally? No, my father was not generally like that. He was extremely passionate and driven.”

She continued, “He could have a temper sometimes, but he did not go around challenging people to fights. Certainly not after he was a teenager. Anyway, he didn’t behave or boast in that way…My father worked extremely hard and directly toward the idea of authentic representation in Hollywood for an Asian man, so I don’t think he would’ve gone around beating up stunt people and that kind of stuff as a way of furthering his cause.”

Tarantino frequently defended the scene, saying that he based his fictional portrayal on real anecdotes about Lee from people who knew the actor.

“Bruce Lee was kind of an arrogant guy,” Tarantino said in a 2019 press conference. “The way he was talking, I didn’t just make a lot of that up. I heard him say things like that to that effect. If people are saying, ‘Well he never said he could beat up Mohammad Ali,’ well yeah he did. Alright? Not only did he say that but his wife, Linda Lee, said that in her first biography I ever read. She absolutely said that.”

The controversy still rears its head sporadically. During a 2021 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Tarantino told critics of the scene to “suck a dick,” with the caveat that he understood why a daughter would object to any negative portrayal of her father.

By the time “The Futher Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” hits select theaters this month (and expands to Netflix in December), more than seven years will have passed since “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” premiered. Perhaps all parties have said everything there is to say about the Bruce Lee scene. But given how much the trailer leans into the matter, we could be in for another round of arguments about the portrayal.

#3564. ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. “Soul Patrol” opens in select theaters from Kino Lorber starting Friday, November 6.

The Vietnam War ended over a half-century ago, but the 20-year war remains a conflict that American artists keep going back to, finding new avenues and perspectives to tackle the many stories of the generation of men who had their lives irrevocably shaped by the conflict. Recent takes have centered the (often-neglected) perspective of the Vietnamese, or — like Spike Lee’s underrated late-career great “Da 5 Bloods” — explored the relatively under-examined service of Black men who served in the war. Related Stories Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52 Emily Feingold Hired as EVP, Communications for The Walt Disney Company

“Soul Patrol,” a new documentary from director J.M. Harper, looks at the Black soldiers of the war through the perspective of Ed Emanuel, a writer who served as a 17-year-old. In his 2003 memoir of the same title, Emanuel described tracking down and reuniting with the men he served with in the first Black special operations Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol team, during his short 1968 to 1969 tour.

“Soul Patrol” finds the men in 2024, in what will be the last reunion they hold. Gathering together, the men — Emanuel, Lawton Mackey, Thad Givens, Emerson Branch, Jesse Lewis, Willie T. Brown, Willie Merkerson, and Norman Reid — sit in the conference room of a Florida hotel to discuss the memories of their service that has stuck with them over the decades, in the hope that their discussion can help them move on.

The opening, and Emmanuel’s narration, help bring context to the small stretch of the war that the film explores. In 1968, as the young men went to serve their country, America itself proved more turbulent than ever; Emanuel was on the plane to Vietnam as Robert F. Kennedy’s assassination was first reported. Protests against the war were growing, and the Civil Rights movement opposed the war as well; a speech from Martin Luther King Jr. becomes a crucial emotional turning point for Emanuel later, as he begins to wonder whether the trauma he experienced serving in the war was worth it.

Through the film, Emanuel and the footage of the reunion between the men guide the audience through their experiences, from the trauma they endured to the discrimination and tokenization they faced as Black soldiers fighting for America. One scene peels back at the men’s conflicting feelings around the nickname for their unit, a racialized moniker that’s simultaneously endearing and patronizing. Others focus on formative experiences Emanuel experiences throughout the war, including a hazy night in Bangkok that’s proves formative both sexually and emotionally.

Harper — whose debut feature “As We Speak” also played at Sundance — has a loud, uncompromisingly blunt style, and the film missteps most clearly when his directorial choices verge on heavy-handed. The film makes clumsy use of actor-led reenactments that are a little too slick and generic to slot seamlessly into the Super 8 footage and actor interviews that make up the bulk of the story. This particularly applies to an opening visual metaphor, in which an old veteran is haunted by a vision of his past, which proves more excessive and obvious than enlightening. Other formal choices feel designed to provoke emotional reactions the material can easily do on its own, particularly a loud, string-heavy score that feels overly generic for the material.

It’s when the film mostly gets out of its own way and lets the men’s experiences do the work that “Soul Patrol” really shines. The Super 8 footage collected from their tour in Vietnam, most of which was shot by the men themselves, is visually arresting and intimate, and Harper frequently employs quick cuts and montages of that on-the-ground film and b-roll of newscasts and ads of the time to flesh out the world they once inhabited. The reunion scenes are simply but artfully shot in black and white, including a revealing conversation among the men’s wives and partners about living with them that gently broadens the perspectives in the film’s portrait.

“Soul Patrol” admirably never tries to sum up the full experience of what Vietnam was, rather just trying to sum up what it was for these men. In the film’s closing stretch, it turns its attention to the men’s difficult experiences returning home from the war, with a candor and a vulnerability that’s hard not to tear up from. As one member of Soul Patrol reflects eloquently towards the end of the film, “We need to tell the stories to look at where we were at, where we come from, and where we headed. You need to know your beginning before you can figure out your ending.”

“Soul Patrol” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Kino Lorber opens the film in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3563. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3562. Who Is Annatar? Sauron's Fair Form Explained

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power introduces Sauron's fair form, Annatar. One of the most famous fictional villains of all time, he may be, but Sauron's physical appearance has always remained somewhat ambiguous. J.R.R. Tolkien describes Sauron in only the vaguest possible terms, and the popularized images of a towering warrior in black armor or a flaming eye atop Barad-dûr come mostly from Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings movie trilogy.

Tolkien gets a little more descriptive about Sauron's appearance in Middle-earth's Second Age, which provides the setting for Amazon's The Rings of Power TV series. In canon, Sauron is licking his wounds following Morgoth's defeat. Upon finally reappearing, he takes the disguise of "Annatar," which Tolkien labels a "fair form" without ever really offering firm details. As Annatar plays a major role in The Rings of Power season 2, here's everything Middle-earth mythology reveals about Sauron's favorite face.

Though best known for his work in the field of warmongering, Sauron began as one of the Maiar - primordial, angel-adjacent, immortal spirits created as servants to the God of Tolkien's world, Eru Ilúvatar. Sauron would be corrupted by Melkor (later known as Morgoth), who was a higher-ranking spirit turned evil through greed, jealousy, and anger. All Maiar possess the ability to assume whatever physical form they desire, and many utilized this gift to mingle unseen among Elves and other Children of Ilúvatar. Sauron had other ideas, and exploited his shape-shifting to create a one-man Halloween party of guises.

During J.R.R. Tolkien's First Age, Sauron would change shape as a means of inspiring fear within his enemies. As the Second Age began, he perhaps realized the opposite would prove more effective, and returned to Middle-earth as "Annatar." Described by Tolkien as a "fair form," the author never offers a clear account of Annatar's handsome visage, but taking into consideration the kingdoms who accepted him as a valued friend, many have logically assumed Sauron's Annatar form was akin to an Elf or Númenórean.

The "Annatar" name was part of Sauron's deception too. The word means "Lord of Gifts" in the Quenya language of Elves - an allusion to how he promised knowledge, glory, wealth, and power to all those who heeded his great wisdom.

Sauron's first order of business as "Annatar" was deceiving the Elves, and duly made for Eregion, where the race's best smiths welcomed him. It's important to note that not all Elves trusted Annatar. The likes of Elrond, Gil-galad and Galadriel all deduced the newcomer's promises were too good to be true, and Annatar wouldn't venture near Lindon or Lothlórien as a result. Furthermore, none of the Elves - not even the suspicious ones - realized the deceitful Annatar was actually Sauron in disguise.

Sauron's purpose in Eregion was creating the Rings of Power. As a Maia, Sauron had served under Aulë, widely considered the god of blacksmiths and worshiped by Dwarves. Consequently, Sauron knew as much about craftsmanship as he did dark magic, and he put both to work while in Eregion. The Elves were keen to craft Rings of Power, and Sauron willingly offered his divine expertise on the matter. As recounted in The Fellowship of the Ring, Sauron betrayed his new friends by weaving a method of corrupting those who wore the Rings into their forging.

The sixteen Rings of Power later held by Dwarves and Men were directly influenced by Annatar. The Elves' three Rings were crafted by Celebrimbor personally, but still using Sauron's sinister method. Annatar then skulked back to Mordor and made his Ruling Ring, and only when Galadriel, Gil-galad and Círdan slipped on their three Rings did the Elves finally realize how badly they'd messed up.

Going into The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3, Sauron should be more or less done with his Annatar disguise. This season picks up after a five-year time jump, with the War of the Elves and Sauron well underway. For much of this time, Sauron's domination seems assured. However, he runs into a significant loss and is eventually taken to Númenor as Ar-Pharazôn's prisoner. In an effort to get on the corrupt king's good side, Sauron takes on a disguise once again. When this plays out on screen, we may get another look at Annatar.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

There's a cloud of ambiguity over which physical form Sauron adopted during his time on the island kingdom. Tolkien's writing heavily suggests the villain once again transformed into a "fair" shape, but never explicitly states whether Sauron recycled Annatar or picked something more befitting for his mortal hosts, and convincing arguments can be made both ways. Whatever he might've looked like, Sauron didn't stick with the "Annatar" moniker, since the people of Númenor already knew his true identity.

As he did with the Elves, Sauron charmed and manipulated those around him in Númenor. Instead of promising gifts and lore, however, he stoked the Númenóreans' existing anger toward the Valar, pushing them toward worshiping Morgoth instead. Sauron rose from a prisoner to Ar-Pharazôn's most valued advisor, ultimately convincing the King to embark on a foolhardy assault on Valinor.

Whether Sauron takes on his Annatar appearance in The Rings of Power season 3 or season 4, the fall of Númenor will, according to Tolkien, mean the definitive end of the Dark Lord's fair form. The massive wave that takes out the island kingdom takes out Sauron's physical body as well, leaving him a formless essence once again. Though he eventually reforms in Mordor, Sauron can never again take on any beautiful or seductive form. His evil must always show through his skin from that point onward. So, the time will come for Annatar to leave us forever.

#3561. 10 Greatest Sam Rockwell Movies, Ranked

With a career spanning over 30 years, Sam Rockwell has established himself as an actor who can disappear into any role. The size of the part never matters, because Rockwell makes five minutes on screen so memorable that it feels like he's the lead star of the movie.

Possessing an effortless charm that adds layers to his dramatic roles and likability to his comedic turns, Rockwell is the actor who elevates any part that he chooses to play. Whether it was as an out-of-control convict in The Green Mile, or as the President of the United States in Vice, Rockwell steals every scene he's in. Ahead of his latest films, Wild Horse Nine and Ray Gunn, the following films showcase Rockwell's skills and serve as a reminder that he's one of the most exciting actors working today.

In The Best of Enemies, Rockwell plays C.P. Ellis, the president of the Ku Klux Klan in 1970s Durham, North Carolina. When the local black school burns down, community organizer Ann Atwater (Taraji P. Henson) and C.P. are forced to work together to establish a peaceful transition into desegregation. Although the two first find it impossible to coexist, they begin to connect, leading to C.P. questioning his values.

Rockwell is no stranger to playing characters with deplorable beliefs, but at least in The Best of Enemies his character is allowed a redemptive journey. Based on the book The Best of Enemies: Race and Redemption in the New South by Osha Gray Davidson, the film sheds light on a lesser-known true story about the lessons learned through desegregation. The Best of Enemies will hit familiar notes of other like-minded movies, but feels fresh based on the strength of the performances from Rockwell and Henson, who work off of one another's energy in both moments of anger and understanding.

Rockwell took the highest office when he appeared as President George W. Bush in the Adam McKay satire, Vice. Following the life and controversies of former Vice President Dick Cheney, (Christian Bale) Vice is a comedy of the darkest nature with biting political commentary. The biographical depiction of Cheney shows his rise to power within the White House, made possible by Bush's invitation to be his running mate.

Rockwell might not be the obvious choice to play President Bush, but with the aid of only a little makeup, he transforms into the former Commander in Chief. The film's core focus is on former Vice President Cheney, but that didn't prevent Rockwell from catching critics' attention with his affable portrayal of Bush. Vice would go on to receive multiple Academy Award nominations, including a Best Supporting Actor nod for Rockwell.

Earlier in his career, Rockwell played a part in another controversial politician's career in the Ron Howard-directed Frost/Nixon. The film, an adaptation of the stage play of the same name by Peter Morgan, tells the story of a series of taped one-on-one interviews between British journalist David Frost (Michael Sheen) and disgraced president Richard Nixon (Frank Langella).

While the film is primarily carried on the strength of Langella and Sheen's performances in their title roles, Rockwell received strong critical praise for his supporting performance as the strong-willed Jim Reston Jr. As an investigator who assists Frost in his preparation for the interviews, Rockwell brings a ferocious intensity as a professor with passionate feelings about Nixon's administration and the crimes he feels the former President wasn't held accountable for. Frost/Nixon gave Rockwell a chance to shine in a large production, and he didn't waste the opportunity.

The offbeat satirical comedy Jojo Rabbit follows a 10-year-old boy, Johannes "Jojo" Betzler (Roman Griffin Davis), who is a loyal member of a Hitler Youth group during the collapse of the Nazi forces. The lonely Jojo spends his time playing with his imaginary friend Hitler (Taika Waititi) and his mother Rosie (Scarlett Johansson), who harbors secret resentment toward the Nazi party. As Jojo tries to prove himself to the local armed forces, he discovers Rosie is hiding a young woman, Elsa (Thomasin McKenzie), from the Nazis.

Rockwell is incredibly funny as the apathetic leader of the Nazi youth, Captain Klenzendorf. Rockwell's embodiment of a soldier disillusioned with both the war and the side he's fighting on is somehow as nuanced in its sorrow as it is broad in its comedy. Klenzendorf isn't in much of Jojo Rabbit, but as is usually the case with Rockwell, the time he's on-screen is electric. His affection for Jojo leads to a few emotionally heartbreaking scenes as Klenzendorf makes his last moments ones to protect his young friend.

One of Rockwell's earliest roles that drew acclaim was his performance in the indie drama Lawn Dogs. The gated community of Camelot Gardens may look pristine from the outside, but the disaffected families that live in its suburban grounds are far from happy. When a member of the community, ten-year-old Devon (Mischa Barton), befriends a groundskeeper, Trent (Rockwell), their innocent friendship sends the wrong message to the wrong people.

Lawn Dogs gave Rockwell one of his first larger roles, and he delivers an understated performance in his interactions with the persistent attempts at friendship by the young Devon. The film approaches scenes within Camelot Gardens in a dreamlike presentation that carries an undertone of menace for every interaction Devon has. The surreal structure of Lawn Dogs might not be for everyone, but fans of Rockwell who haven't seen it should make the time.

A coming-of-age story gives Rockwell one of his most charming roles in the dramedy The Way, Way Back. The film follows Duncan (Liam James), a 14-year-old boy who is forced into a summer vacation with his mother Pam (Toni Collette) and her volatile boyfriend Trent (Steve Carell). With his mother wrapped up in her relationship, Duncan explores their vacation spot and meets Owen (Rockwell), a man who works at the local water park. The two develop a bond, and Owen offers him a summer job to help at the park.

Rockwell channels his best Bill Murray in Meatballs while providing mentorship to a boy he can tell needs a friend. Rockwell's relaxed charisma is on full display for every scene in The Way, Way Back, and his natural comic timing makes it surprising that he didn't do more traditional comedies. Everyone in the cast does a great job in this rewatchable gem, but Rockwell will be the reason viewers come back to The Way, Way Back for a second or third watch.

One of the movies Rockwell fans commonly point to as their favorite is the slow-burn sci-fi drama Moon. Sam Bell (Rockwell) is close to finishing up his three-year contract as the sole operator of a space station, but he begins to suspect his situation may be more dire than he assumed. As Sam pulls on the thread of his own existence, he finds that what he knew to be the truth was all an elaborate lie.

Without including any spoilers for Moon, the film is a wholly original mystery that continues to develop with satisfying reveals. A movie starring one person can be daunting to watch, but Rockwell is compelling throughout the runtime, and the film doesn't lag thanks to his performance. Even if viewers guess some of the plot twists in advance, it doesn’t take away from Sam’s emotional fallout from the discoveries.

The lonely last stop before execution is the setting for the supernatural drama The Green Mile. Paul Edgecomb (Tom Hanks) oversees the normally mundane death row in a 1930s prison, but that all changes with the arrival of a kind and gentle inmate named John Coffey (Michael Clarke Duncan). Coffey was convicted of the brutal murder of two young girls, but the crime doesn’t match the sweet-natured disposition of the man awaiting execution. As Paul learns the truth behind the crimes, he'll find his life forever changed.

Even though he has a small role in The Green Mile, Rockwell commands the screen for every second as the wild and feral prisoner William "Wild Bill" Wharton. Wild Bill is the polar opposite of Coffey, continually disruptive and violent without any remorse for the crimes that landed him on death row. Even though Rockwell exudes charm naturally, he brings none to one of his most chaotic characters.

An underrated classic that doesn't get the attention it deserves, Confessions of a Dangerous Mind was an early opportunity to show what Rockwell looked like as a leading man. Based on the autobiography of the same name, Confessions of a Dangerous Mind tells the life story of game show producer Chuck Barris (Rockwell). According to Barris, he allegedly worked as a spy and government assassin while creating some of television's most popular shows, like The Dating Game and The Newlywed Game.

The part of Chuck Barris made its way around Hollywood with multiple names attached, but it was when George Clooney took over as director that he lobbied for Rockwell to play the eccentric producer. Although the studio was skeptical of casting the then-unknown Rockwell, he would eventually secure the part of Barris and receive critical acclaim for his dynamic and energetic portrayal. This is an absolute must-watch for any fans of Rockwell.

A grieving mother will not be ignored in the award-winning drama, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. The film follows Mildred Hayes (Frances McDormand), a frustrated and heartbroken mother to a daughter who was raped and murdered by an unknown assailant. Fed up with the ineptitude of the local police, Mildred posts messages about her daughter's case on billboards near town to demand attention. As the presence of the billboards brings negative attention to her, she relentlessly pursues the truth.

As one of the police officers opposing Mildred's billboard, Jason Dixon is one of Rockwell's crowning achievements. As the movie goes on, the boorish exterior of Dixon is continually pulled away in small pieces, revealing a man who is struggling to hide his own pain and disappointment until he has no choice but to look within. Rockwell's role as the violent and stubborn Officer Dixon would win him his first and only (so far) Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor.

A mother personally challenges the local authorities to solve her daughter's murder when they fail to catch the culprit.

#3560. ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

For one of the most important screenings of “To Hold a Mountain,” the filmmakers had to bring their own electricity. In July, co-directors Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić hauled a tent, a generator, and a DCP up to the Montenegrin highlands where they had spent years filming.

The creative couple, also partnered in life, wanted the shepherds who lived and worked in Sinjajevina to see the movie they had made possible. But by then, Montenegro had already resolved their story’s central conflict — scrapping the government’s plan to turn these people’s ancestral pastures into a military training ground after joining NATO in 2017. Related Stories ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

“To Hold a Mountain” won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize for documentary at Sundance, and Montenegro’s prime minister and president even showed up to the shepherds’ screening with their families, unannounced. When the film opens at New York’s Film Forum on December 16, American audiences will see the feature’s updated conclusion.

“We reopened the film to continue shooting and then a second end happened that was very empowering and powerful,” Tutorov said at IndieWire’s Art of the Doc series.

During our conversation, the filmmaker recalled arriving in Sinjajevina with Glomazić on the first day of protest. They wanted to help the community and make a movie, and agreed early on that those were two different jobs.

“We will separate our activist mission from our filmmaker’s mission,” she said. “That was a very good decision because it allowed us to be very bold in both roles.”

Onscreen, the fight over who would get to lay claim to the mountain centered on two people who already did: Gara, a shepherd and community leader, and Nada, the young girl she was raising. As the threat to their home brought a history of violence in their own family to the surface, the directors had to reckon with how much of Nada’s private life might become public.

“We really wanted it to be an empowering experience for [her],” Tutorov said.

Nada was twelve and a half when the filmmakers began to understand what the story would ask of her, and Tutorov said they decided to keep filming until she turned eighteen — precisely so Nada could decide for herself whether she wanted to be part of it. The crew logged more than 230 shooting days, though some yielded only half an hour of footage.

Gara and Nada had work to do, too. The directors and cinematographer Eva Kraljević shared a small shepherd’s shed, assisting with various chores including cows that had to be milked twice a day. Over successive summers, their routine became a framing device. Tutorov, who studied art history, thinks of the mountain as a kind of chorus bearing witness to living things on it.

Last July, just as the filmmakers were wrapping up, Montenegro’s government canceled the training-ground plan. Tutorov believes “To Hold a Mountain” and how it told the existing community’s story influenced that decision. She also pointed out that a different government was in power by 2025, following years of organizing by Sinjajevina locals.

At the shepherd’s screening a year later, Prime Minister Milojko Spajić said the film reinforced his view that canceling the plan had been the right call. Then Montenegro chose “To Hold a Mountain” as its official submission for the international feature Oscar. Tutorov said there was irony in realizing that, after years of fighting the government, she and Glomazić would be proudly representing the country on a global stage.

“It feels like they really kind of destroyed our strategy,” she said, warmly.

It’s a good joke, and an even better reason to remember that rough-and-tumble showing. For an evening, the people who’d spent years making their case to the government got to host its leaders on the very land they’d fought to keep. Tutorov recalled what Montenegro’s president told the filmmakers after seeing the movie: “Thank you guys for teaching us democracy.”

Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu.Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us onFacebook,Twitter,Instagram, and YouTube.

#3559. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.
