Fantastic Beasts And Where To Find Them (2016)

Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes Of Grindelwald (2018)

Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets Of Dumbledore (2022)

The one that started it all established the series' structure with this Harry Potter movie length of two-and-a-half hours. In the film, Harry Potter learns his parents were great wizards, and receives an invitation to study at Hogwarts, a prestigious wizarding school. Daniel Radcliffe took on the role of Harry Potter at the young age of 12, along with fellow child actors Emma Watson and Rupert Grint. The cast was rounded out by some of Britain's top acting talent, and the film went on to an impressive $1 billion at the box office for director Chris Columbus.

Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone is the shortest book in J.K. Rowling's series but boasts one of the longer Harry Potter film lengths. Despite this, numerous beloved characters like Peeves were still cut from the final product. That said, Columbus' first two movies are the most faithful adaptations of the books, leaving out only what could be considered extraneous (Peeves aside) and following Rowling's narrative beats almost to a T. The runtime reflects this fact as, at times, Sorcerer's Stone can run at a glacial pace compared to the relatively quick read that is the book.

Released one year after Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone, Chris Columbus finished up his two-film run with Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, and the Harry Potter movie runtimes increased. Columbus had previously worked well with children as a director on films like Home Alone and a writer on The Goonies, so he was perfect to launch the franchise. This second movie showed what dangers Harry faced in the future as the past of Lord Voldemort, the franchise's main antagonist, is delved into.

The film made $882 million and was the second highest-grossing film of 2002.

Much like Sorcerer's Stone, Chamber of Secrets and its ending stick relatively close to the source material. Of what was cut were various encounters with secondary antagonist Gilderoy Lockhart that only further served to enforce his buffoonery and much of Percy Weasley's role in the narrative. Of all the Harry Potter film lengths, Chamber of Secrets is the longest and is sometimes regarded as the worst Harry Potter movie. Chamber of Secrets exacerbates Sorcerer's Stone's pacing issues, but at least Harry is seen actually performing magic in this film, and popular characters like Lucius Malfoy and Dobby are introduced.

Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban has a complex ending and while Columbus made his Harry Potter movies mostly about children discovering magic, Academy Award-winning director Alfonso Cuarón (Gravity) took the helm for this one and made one of the most adult films in the series — with one of the shorter Harry Potter movie runtimes. Cuarón cut back the runtime, although it was still over two hours. Sirius Black, a man once held at the Azkaban prison, was introduced as Harry's godfather, and the film changed the franchise's tone drastically.

Prisoner of Azkaban is widely regarded as the best Harry Potter movie in the series, even though Voldemort isn't in it at all. The film moves at breakneck speed without sacrificing important exposition and its noticeable tonal shift was necessary to usher in Goblet of Fire, as the Harry Potter stories themselves grew darker with each subsequent book. However, with the cut runtime came cut characters — and no Quidditch — and side characters like Neville, Dean, or Seamus had minimal screen time.

Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire really showed that character deaths could be serious in the series, but with one of the middling Harry Potter movie runtimes, audiences experienced major cuts for the first time. In this film, Harry Potter took part in a Triwizard Tournament that saw him battle in a series of tests to determine which school had the best young wizard. However, that was just to move the plot along as the true importance of this movie, directed by Mike Newell, was to bring Lord Voldemort back from the dead.

Despite having a runtime of almost 2 hours and 40 minutes, Goblet of Fire was the first Harry Potter film that saw huge cuts to the narrative to reach its conclusion while still providing enough exposition. For starters, fans who have only watched the Harry Potter movies have never heard of Ludo Bagman, Hermione's House Elf rights campaign, the importance of Winky the House Elf, or how Barty Crouch Jr. managed to escape Azkaban and eventually orchestrate his evil plan. Had the Goblet of Fire runtime been expanded, certain things would've made more sense going forward.

While Order of the Phoenix is the longest Harry Potter book, it is the shortest in terms of Harry Potter movie runtimes. David Yates directed this film and remained with the franchise to the end. This movie saw the rise of the powerful Order of the Phoenix to battle the Death Eaters, and Harry learned who his real allies were. This was the step in Harry's journey where he found himself betrayed, as the Ministry of Magic refused to believe Voldemort was back and left the Order to fight alone.

Thanks to Goblet of Fire, fans of the novels were prepared for how much cutting Order of the Phoenix would undergo. Despite this, it seems almost criminal that the longest book in the series got the shortest runtime. Much of Harry's inner turmoil and scenes that displayed his increasingly troubling connection to Voldemort didn't appear, with the attack on Mr. Weasley being one of the only major instances included. Because of its short runtime, Harry's angst is downplayed to a degree, and the most integral part of Snape's worst memory doesn't happen.

Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince arrived in 2009 and added a new twist to the story, as Dumbledore's close companion proved to be a possible Death Eater sent into Hogwarts. Snape, the Half-Blood Prince, left a notebook behind that Harry found and used to aid him through the year. By the end of Half-Blood Prince, things looked dire as the Death Eaters began to infiltrate Hogwarts. While Voldemort demands that Draco Malfoy kill Dumbledore with the wand tied to him, it's Snape who steps forward and murders the headmaster, taking away Harry's beloved mentor.

While Half-Blood Prince has one of the more appropriate Harry Potter movie runtimes, Voldemort's backstory could still have been expanded upon. The film only includes two out of the seven memories that relate to Voldemort's overall backstory, which would've included how he procured the locket, cup, and ring Horcruxes, the Gaunt family, and Tom Riddle's gradual decline into Voldemort. However, Yates decided to keep the Half-Blood Prince runtime down to about the same length as Goblet of Fire, with the latter being slightly longer.

The final book in the Harry Potter series is Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, and it was split into two movies, both having some of the shorter Harry Potter movie runtimes. The first of the films came out in 2010 and saw Harry, Hermione, and Ron on the run after the death of Dumbledore. This entire movie focuses on the relationship between the three leads as their friendship fractures, breaks, and is eventually mended to make them stronger than ever as they return to battle Voldemort and the Death Eaters to end the war once and for all.

Splitting The Deathly Hallows into two movies worked well for covering the final book, and the film cut off the story at the perfect place. Due to having two films to tell the entire tale, much of what happened in The Deathly Hallows book was included. The only thing that felt somewhat pushed to the wayside was Dumbledore's backstory and how Harry wrestled with that relationship and trust. In addition, Harry's internal struggle between pursuing the Hallows and the Horcruxes wasn't addressed in the tight two and a half hours.

The final movie in the initial Harry Potter franchise saw Harry and his friends join forces with the wizards that had survived the Death Eaters. It was the Battle of Hogwarts, and everyone gathered to take on the villains and save their school. Most characters had their heroic moments, many beloved heroes died in battle, and Harry had his final battle with Voldemort to end the war and save his school. By the final scene, Harry was allowed to live happily ever after. Concerning the Harry Potter movie runtimes, this movie was shorter than any other in the series.

Despite having the shortest of all the Harry Potter movie runtimes, Deathly Hallows Part 2 covered the second half of the novel well and ended the series on a bombastic note. Certain elements were changed from the book for the better, with Harry and Voldemort's final battle being much more action-packed and taking place in the courtyard rather than the Great Hall. The only unfortunate part of this was that the tight runtime didn't allow proper impact for major character deaths like Fred, Lupin, and Tonks.

Five years after the Harry Potter franchise, the Wizarding World came back to the big screen, but the film wasn't based on books and was instead a story J.K. Rowling created for cinema. Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them told the story of Newt Scamander, whose books about fantastic beasts Harry studied in school. Newt is an adult fascinated with the fantastic beasts in the world. However, this series had a bigger arc — the rise of Grindelwald. These Harry Potter movie runtimes were still over two hours, but not as long as many of the earlier films.

The Fantastic Beasts franchise started out strong, and audiences welcomed the new protagonist Newt Scamander with open arms. No books to follow meant runtimes would tell the proper amount of story in the proper amount of time, and the future of Fantastic Beasts seemed bright. While it was clear that Rowling's talents as a screenwriter didn't match that of her authorship, the film's runtime felt comfortable and introduced new magic into the franchise along with an entirely different setting and time period.

Fantastic Beasts and the Crimes of Grindelwald is only slightly longer than the first movie. This was the second movie in the Fantastic Beasts series, and while Newt Scamander was still the main protagonist, there was a lot here to set up a battle mentioned in the original Harry Potter movies between Albus Dumbledore and his greatest rival, Gellert Grindelwald. This saw both Jude Law and Johnny Depp arrive as Dumbledore and Grindelwald, but the movie was mostly a set-up for the upcoming battle with Grindelwald preparing to start a Wizarding War with humanity.

Crimes of Grindelwald is famously where the Fantastic Beasts franchise went wrong, and while the runtime was longer, it still didn't give enough breathing room for audiences to understand the complexity of the plot with one watch. The second Fantastic Beasts movie was packed to the brim with information and tie-ins to Harry Potter which worked more to its detriment than its success. Canon was retconned many times and despite only being two minutes longer than the first film, Crimes of Grindelwald felt much longer.

#3536. Man High On Meth Kills Mom, Believed She Was Possessed

An Oregon man who believed his mother was demonically possessed while he was high on meth has been sentenced to life in prison for her murder ... and prosecutors say he had been thinking about killing her for weeks.

38-year-old Ronald Kirk was convicted of second-degree murder and felony possession of a firearm after shooting and killing his 61-year-old mother, Rosa Leyva, inside the home they shared.

Kirk had been living with his mother in her small Gladstone, Oregon home ... but according to FOX12, their relationship was anything but peaceful.

Prosecutors say Leyva had been fed up with her son's drug and alcohol use, explosive temper, and increasingly bizarre behavior ... and by November 2024, she was ready to kick him out.

According to Clackamas County prosecutors, Kirk had become obsessed with exorcisms and demonic possession while using meth ... even telling a friend he believed his own mother was possessed.

And here's where things get even more disturbing.

A month before the murder, Kirk allegedly left a voicemail for his son claiming his grandmother was possessed ... and admitting he had "almost" put a bullet in her head the day before.

Meanwhile, Leyva was becoming increasingly fearful of her son.

On Nov. 8, she sent Kirk a text making it clear she wanted him gone, writing, "You need to leave. I don't want anyone in my house."

There was just one problem ... Kirk had no job, no money, and was financially dependent on his mother.

Between Nov. 8 and Nov. 11, Leyva contacted Gladstone police asking for help because she was afraid of what her son might do.

In home surveillance footage from Nov. 11, later shown to jurors, Leyva could be heard pleading with her son to get help.

"You're higher than a kite. Get some help. Please," she told him.

Sadly, just two weeks later, her worst fears became reality.

On Nov. 26, 2024, Leyva failed to show up for work, immediately raising concerns among her coworkers and friends, who knew about her son's troubling behavior.

When they couldn't get in contact with her, police were called to conduct a welfare check ... and what officers discovered inside the home was horrifying.

Kirk answered the door and casually told officers his mother was inside and hadn't been conscious for about a day.

When officers entered, they found Leyva dead at the dining room table, sitting in front of her laptop with a full glass of wine nearby. Her body was covered in pillowcases, and she had suffered a single gunshot wound to the head.

Investigators later determined Leyva had been killed around 6:45 PM on Nov. 25 ... meaning Kirk had remained inside the home with his mother's body for nearly 24 hours.

"He sat there with his mother's dead body for a full day," Senior Deputy District Attorney Rusty Amos told jurors.

During Kirk's sentencing, his two sons delivered emotional statements about losing their grandmother ... but they had very different messages for their father.

One son, Andre Leyva, told Kirk he had chosen to forgive him despite everything.

"I forgive you. I love you because that's what God does, and I hope prison and God have mercy on your soul," he said.

His older brother, Antonio Leyva, wasn't ready to offer that same forgiveness.

"I know others have already forgiven you, but I am very far from that. And my Grandma Leyva, I don't just miss her; it's more than that," he told the court.

As for Kirk, he told the court he plans to appeal his conviction.

"I was convicted of second-degree murder," Kirk said before sentencing. "I understand and so I'm ready to be sentenced off and close this case."

Kirk was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 25 years ... meaning he'll be in his early 60s before he even has a chance at freedom.

#3535. Forget ‘Twin Peaks,’ Ben Affleck’s Forgotten 7-Episode Mystery Was Ahead of Its Time

Amanda M. Castro is a Network TV writer at Collider and a New York–based journalist whose work has appeared in Newsweek, where she is an Associate Editor, and The U.S. Sun, where she previously served as a Senior Consumer Reporter.

She specializes in network television coverage, delivering sharp, thoughtful analysis of long-running procedural hits and ambitious new dramas across broadcast TV. At Collider, Amanda explores character arcs, storytelling trends, and the cultural impact of network series that keep audiences tuning in week after week.

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Amanda is bilingual and holds a degree in Communication, Film, and Media Studies from the University of New Haven.

Ben Affleck is having quite the moment on Netflix. His latest thriller, Animals, has held the No. 1 spot on the streamer's global English-language movie chart for four consecutive weeks, pulling in another 4.7 million views and 8.4 million hours watched between October 26 and November 1, 2026. But long before his latest streaming success, Affleck tried his hand at something completely different: creating one of network television's strangest mystery series.

In 2002, Affleck and his producing partner Sean Bailey co-created Push, Nevada, a surreal mystery about a mild-mannered IRS agent who stumbles into a desert town filled with corruption, cryptic clues, and slow-dancing strangers. It sounded like Twin Peaks meets The X-Files — until ABC added one wild twist: Viewers could win a million dollars by solving the mystery themselves. The result was a show too ambitious, too strange, and too ahead of its time to survive more than seven episodes.

Push, Nevada followed Jim Prufrock (Derek Cecil), an accountant who receives a mysterious fax suggesting embezzlement at the Versailles Casino. When he heads to Push — a nowhere town drenched in neon and paranoia — he discovers that its residents haven’t filed a tax return since 1985 and that an ominous company, Watermark LLC, seems to control everything from the police to the local dive bar. Oddballs populated the noir-ish mystery: Scarlett Chorvat’s Mary, a “Slo-dancer” warning Prufrock to get out while he still can; Jon Polito’s corrupt casino boss; and Armand Assante’s slick criminal known only as “Mr. Smooth.”

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

It looked incredible, with cinematography by Jim Denault, known for Boys Don’t Cry, and a moody palette of reds, golds, and shadows. Critics compared its tone and aesthetic directly to David Lynch’s Twin Peaks — from the quirky characters to the eerie score and slightly stilted dialogue. But while Lynch’s small-town surrealism invited obsession, Push, Nevada asked for something even stranger: participation.

Each episode contained hidden clues — web addresses, code words, even on-screen numbers — leading viewers closer to a real-life prize of $1,045,000. Fans could follow the story across fake websites, emails, and even physical mailers in what producers dubbed “the three-ball theory” of engagement: viewers could wade in, swim, or dive deep. The experiment made Push, Nevada one of the earliest examples of transmedia storytelling on network TV.

Unfortunately, it also made it unwatchable for casual audiences. The mystery was dense, the tone self-serious, and the clues often so obvious (highlighted in red boxes during reruns) that the whole thing felt like homework. Competing against CSI and Will & Grace, Push, Nevada was canceled after seven episodes — though ABC still had to finish the contest legally. The winner, New Jersey native Mark Nakamoto, solved the final puzzle and claimed the million-dollar prize, but the show itself vanished into cult TV history.

The longtime friends have something bigger in mind for their next chapter.

Today, Push, Nevada feels like a bizarre artifact from the early 2000s — part prestige mystery, part ARG, part marketing stunt. However, despite its flaws, it accurately predicted how audiences would one day crave deeper, more interactive storytelling through shows, websites, and games.

#3531. John Ternus talks plans to improve Siri AI

During Apple’s quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus was asked repeatedly about Siri AI’s future. Here’s what he said about Apple’s plans for improving and expanding Siri AI.

Sometimes when Apple launches a new feature or product, the company sees its work as finished, and whatever ships goes unchanged for far too long. Many might characterize Siri this way, arguing the assistant went years without meaningful improvement or updates.

But according to Apple CEO John Ternus, the Siri AI that just shipped is only the beginning of what’s planned.

Yesterday on Apple’s quarterly earnings call, Ternus gave a rundown of Siri AI’s capabilities. He concluded: “We’re really excited to have rolled all these innovations out, and there’s still so much more we plan to do.”

This signals that Apple doesn’t see Siri AI as a feature that can now be left alone for a while. Instead, as we already saw in iOS 27.2 last week, Apple is focused on rapidly improving it.

Now that Siri AI is out, I would like to see it iterate as follows:

Support for a wider range of file types, such as PDF.

Accessing it from Search (especially on the Mac) should be instantaneous and reliable.

Proactively suggesting and reminding the user based on what it knows.

What are those future plans? It sounds like agentic capabilities may be among them. Ternus said:

With Siri AI, we really have the kind of—the Siri we always wanted. It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern, orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand capabilities over time.

It’s telling that Ternus says Siri is “primarily request-based today” and mentions “room to expand capabilities” before pivoting to mention agentic features. It sounds like Apple is already, behind-the-scenes, envisioning and working toward a version of Siri that won’t need to be “primarily request-based.”

Finally, later in the call when discussing opportunities for services growth, including potentially launching new services, Ternus says: “We think intelligence is going to be another opportunity as well.” This refers back to an earlier discussion of Apple’s intent to charge a fee for expanded usage limits on certain Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities. The idea is that as Siri evolves and improves, Apple will have opportunities to charge for certain features.

#3529. This TP-Link Wi-Fi 7 Travel Router Is 27% Off for This Early Black Friday Deal

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3527. iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving

iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.

I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters.

My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.

In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.

Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.

iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums, the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple:

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos

Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.

#3526. Charlie Hunnam’s ‘Sons Of Anarchy Meets Money Heist’ Series Adapts Award-Winning Comics

Sons of Anarchy premiered almost two decades ago. Yet, it remains one of the most loved and highly quoted crime dramas of the 21st century. While many factors contributed to the show's success, it was Charlie Hunnam's performance as Jax Teller that truly made it memorable. Hunnam is also all set to return in a new Sons of Anarchy spin-off series, Legends.

However, before that, he will serve as one of the main leads of a promising crime drama on Prime Video. The upcoming crime drama in question, titled Criminal, could become one of the biggest hits in the genre because it adapts a highly acclaimed comic book series of the same name. It already has a lot going in its favor and even its first teaser looks incredibly promising.

Charlie Hunnam has an incredible range as an actor. However, he truly seems to thrive when he serves as the lead in crime thrillers like Sons of Anarchy and The Gentlemen. Owing to this, it is hard not to be excited about what he will bring to the table with his performance in Criminal. What makes the upcoming series even more exciting is that it has one big advantage over many adaptations out there.

Many TV adaptations end up drifting away from their source material. The original creators of their stories end up having little to no involvement in their development. Prime Video's Criminal, however, is taking the completely opposite approach. All installments of the original Criminal comics have been written by Ed Brubaker and illustrated by Sean Philips.

Ed Brubaker himself serves as the Prime Video adaptation's co-showrunner alongside novelist Jordan Harper. With Brubaker's direct involvement with the series as one of its showrunners, Prime Video's Criminal is bound to succeed.

Like the original Criminal comics, the Prime Video series will gradually uncover a massive shared underworld where generations of criminal families are interconnected through heists and never-ending cycles of violence. In the series, Charlie Hunnam is set to play a clever but extremely careful thief who avoids resorting to any kind of violence during his heists.

The Prime Video show will adapt two major arcs from the comics in season 1: Coward and Lawless. While Coward will be about a heist gone wrong, Lawless will feature Luke Evans and Emilia Clarke as leads, following a man's efforts to save his brother. Since Ed Brubaker is the series' showrunner, he will likely ensure that its story closely follows his award-winning comics.

The first look of Prime Video's Criminal is already out. While it may be too soon to draw any conclusions, the series already looks incredibly promising. It features high-stakes robbery scenes that remind one of some of the most compelling heist thrillers, like Money Heist. Meanwhile, the violence and hinted betrayals portrayed in the trailer make it reminiscent of Sons of Anarchy's R-rated crime drama.

Even the show's cast includes many big names, like Adria Arjona, Michael Mando, Richard Jenkins, and John Hawkes, along with Charlie Hunnam and Emilia Clarke. Criminal already comes off as a prestige crime thriller, and its source material has enough content for at least three full seasons.

If all goes well for the Prime Video series, it could find its place among the streaming service's best small-screen offerings. Since Ed Brubaker serves as one of its showrunners, Criminal could even extend far beyond its source material and match the legacy of shows like Sons of Anarchy.

Based on the comic series, Criminal is an action crime series developed by Ed Brubaker and Jordan Harper for Prime Video. This adaptation follows various characters within and adjacent to a bustling criminal underworld and comprises several arcs that occasionally intersect. The series was greenlit by Amazon in 2024.

#3523. Captain Kirk’s Greatest Star Trek Quote Still Hasn't Been Beaten 60 Years Later

Star Trek officially turned 60 this year. Six decades is an impressive milestone by any standard, even for a franchise that's no stranger to landmark accomplishments. In a nice bit of symmetry, "Balance of Terror," an episode widely regarded as one of The Original Series' finest hours (no runtime pun intended), celebrates its own diamond anniversary next month. Written by Paul Schneider and directed by Vincent McEveety, Season 1, Episode 14 introduces the Romulans — who'd go on to become prominent and compelling adversaries — through a tense cat-and-mouse hunt between Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner) and an unnamed Romulan commander (Mark Lenard, also known for playing Sarek in Star Trek: The Next Generation).

Like any piece of entertainment, present or past, elements of Gene Roddenberry's genre-changing hit split into either timeless or critique-worthy time capsules (when they don't overlap). Schneider's script was born out of the Cold War and modeled after submarine movies: psychological and tactical suspense, mystery, secrecy, paranoia, and the likelihood of self-sacrificial stakes. Hand-in-hand with Trek's innate tradition of sci-fi allegories ranging from profound to imperfect to grievous missteps, "Balance of Terror" makes prejudice its focal point — and from that thematic centerpiece emerges a defining quote from the Enterprise's Captain himself.

At this point in Trek history, the Earth-Romulan War had ended roughly a century earlier with a treaty and the creation of the Neutral Zone, a demilitarized segment of space separating the Federation and the Romulan Star Empire. No living human or Romulan has ever laid eyes upon one another. Both civilizations work according to reputation and inference only: the Romulans as cruel, despotic, militaristic conquerors, and to quote Spock (Leonard Nimoy), "Only the Romulans know what they think of Earth." Lieutenant Stiles (Paul Comi), a single-episode Starfleet officer, despises the Romulans sight-unseen because his enlisted ancestors perished during the conflict.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Three — soon to be four — disintegrated Earth outposts along the Federation's Neutral Zone border force the Enterprise to hover dangerously close to the forbidden. They literally can't see the responsible vessel, a Romulan Bird of Prey, thanks to the warship's cloaking device. Once Kirk and his bridge crew manage to spy on the ship's interior, Stiles directs his xenophobic vitriol toward Spock — who's more surprised by the Vulcan and Romulan resemblance than anyone. Stiles accuses Spock of being a spy in the way of every muttered insult that's designed to be heard. Kirk quietly commands the lieutenant to repeat his accusation loudly and clearly before issuing an unassailable reprimand: "Leave any bigotry in your quarters. There's no room for it on the bridge."

The sociopolitical drive behind Roddenberry's concept and multicultural crew isn't news to anyone with at least a passing Star Trek familiarity. Trek's prevailing ideals are intensely sincere, even when the series stumbles into its most heavy-handed and faulty moments (which isn't an excuse for those missteps). "Balance of Terror" remains fascinating precisely because it's unambiguous, riveting, and effective. Stiles' disdain for Spock proves not every future human has, in fact, evolved past bigoted hatred and supremacy into widespread acceptance.

Schneider compounds Kirk's rebuke through a series of pointed, poignant moments: the crew debating the morality of the Enterprise striking against the Bird of Prey, Lieutenant Uhura (Nichelle Nichols) replacing Stiles at the helm, Kirk volunteering to beam the Commander's wounded crew aboard the Enterprise, and his foe's famously mournful compliment once they finally speak face-to-face over the hailing screens. "I regret that we meet in this way," the Commander says, simultaneously a methodical strategist and resigned to his battle-weary life. "You and I are of a kind. In a different reality, I could have called you friend." Kirk's words carry weight because the entire episode preemptively shoulders six decades of Star Trek's keenly attuned resonance — reaching for empathy, respect, teamwork, and communication over every manifestation of their destructive opposites.

#3516. Disney+'s 95-Episode Sci-Fi Series Delivers A Masterclass In Comic Book Adaptations

As far as comic book adaptations go, Disney+ delivered a sci-fi masterpiece consisting of 95 episodes and counting. In the modern streaming landscape, TV shows based on comic book properties tend to be shorter in length. Even the best comic book TV shows, be it Loki or Watchmen, have less than 20 episodes between them. The same can be said for the likes of WandaVision, Wonder Man, or, more recently, the DCU’s Lanterns. Now more than ever, shorter-form content is dominating superhero media on TV.

For that reason, the best of the genre tend to stand out as longer stories. One of Disney+’s best sci-fi shows epitomizes this, given it has had 95 episodes and more planned for the future. The show in question is a two-in-one: X-Men: The Animated Series and X-Men ‘97. The former ran for 76 episodes in the 1990s before the latter was reborn on Disney+ as a continuation. Currently, X-Men ‘97 has 19 episodes across two seasons, continuing the legacy of one of the greatest comic book adaptations. Moreover, X-Men ‘97 season 3 is on the horizon, promising more in the future.

What makes these shows special is their length, allowing characters, storylines, and multi-season arcs to be fully fleshed out, without the need to tie into a wider shared universe. Although both do exist in continuity with other Marvel animated TV shows, they are primarily self-contained, allowing for a much more in-depth exploration of the titular team, their conflicts, villains, and relationship dynamics. On top of all that, X-Men: The Animated Series and X-Men ‘97 tell great adaptations of comic book stories with a mix of fidelity and enough original content to warrant existing. Undoubtedly, the collective whole is a sci-fi, comic book masterpiece.

The two X-Men shows may already be considered masterpieces, but that is only set to be solidified. X-Men ‘97 specifically was revered for the maturity of its writing and the complex way in which it dealt with typical mutant storylines linked to oppression, prejudice, and discrimination. With that in mind, it becomes even more exciting that the show will have at least two more seasons. Season 3 is expected in 2027, while development is ongoing on season 4, priming it for a 2028 release date. Evidently, Disney+’s comic book masterpiece does not intend to slow down.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

That is without mentioning the other promising possibilities of the X-Men franchise on Disney+. After 2026, the mutants will be an official part of live-action stories in the MCU. While this has led to a movie set for release in 2028, it opens the door to plenty of Disney+ stories after Avengers: Secret Wars soft reboots the multiverse.

What this all means is that Marvel Studios could have a sub-franchise that, ironically, could be just as big, if not bigger, than the MCU itself. After all, the roster of X-Men and their many villains is huge, much bigger than that of the Avengers. This offers Marvel a wealth of potential stories that could benefit from a TV format. As proven by X-Men: The Animated Series and X-Men ‘97, longer stories elevate the characters they involve, which could be the same for live-action adaptations.

Marvel Studios has recently overhauled its TV productions, leaning more into traditional serialized formats than the aforementioned short-length seasons that work more as drawn-out movies in a larger universe. If this benefits any of Marvel’s many properties, it is the X-Men franchise. Be it solo character entries centered on the team’s biggest heroes or team-up TV shows akin to X-Men: The Animated Series and X-Men ‘97, Disney+’s comic book masterclass can be extended and adapted in live-action with a host of exciting possibilities.

#3514. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

#3513. Narnia’s Most Debated Ending Isn’t the Problem Fans Think It Is

Anyone who has thoroughly read through C.S. Lewis' The Chronicles of Narnia series will probably know the basics of the story and how religion played a big role in shaping it. They will also be aware that the final novel, The Last Battle, is missing one pivotal character: Susan Pevensie.

For years, many have criticized Lewis for his decision to leave the daughter of Eve out of Aslan's Country, a decision that the author must have known would rile folks up in the end. But while this creative choice was certainly intentional, it is by no means the "problem" that authors like Philip Pullman claim it to be. In fact, it proves that they, like Susan herself, entirely missed the point, and her absence is much more fitting when properly contextualized.

Near the end of the novel, the Earth-based "Friends of Narnia" — Peter, Edmund, and Lucy, their cousin Eustace, his friend Jill, their mentor Digory Kirke, and his childhood friend Polly Plummer — arrive to help King Tirian at the end of Narnian history. Peter banishes the demon Tash just before Aslan ushers all who were faithful to him into Aslan's Country. Not only do we discover that Susan is absent from the group, but we later learn that all but she were killed in a train accident in their world, including Mr. and Mrs. Pevensie. This is why Aslan allows them all to stay in his heavenly realm. Of course, this also means that Susan, who has since turned her back on Narnia, is now without her family in the "real world."

At the end of Prince Caspian, Aslan had told Peter and Susan that they would not return to the fantasy world. While Peter still clung to those years they served as Narnian royalty, Susan let them go entirely. In the twelfth chapter of The Last Battle, Eustace reveals that Susan now views Narnia as "funny games [they] used to play" during childhood. Jill further describes her priorities as "nothing nowadays except nylons and lipstick and invitations." Lastly, Polly adds that the former Queen of Narnia had "wasted all her school time wanting to be the age she is now," stating that she ought to truly grow up in a more authentic sense. Whatever your initial feelings on the matter, Lewis uses this revelation as a moment to pause and reflect on something he has actually been trying to say since the first Narnian chronicle.

Lewis famously dedicated The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe to his goddaughter, Lucy Barfield. Although he finished the book too late for her to enjoy it in childhood, he hoped that she would one day “be old enough to start reading fairy tales again.” It is with this idea in mind that we must reflect on Susan, who seemingly grew too “adult” for Narnia by maturing into a woman who could not leave the Shadowlands behind. While common critiques suggest that Lewis simply misunderstands Susan's mature desires, her decision is not (contrary to popular belief) about sex, nor is it an inherently misogynistic problem on the author's part. After all, Lucy, Jill, and Polly all remain faithful. Rather, the author juxtaposes the Friends' longing for "another country" (the spiritual) with Susan’s obsession with the tangibility of the present (the material). Instead of reflecting well on the lessons Aslan taught, she let them pass her by.

Tragically, this is largely in step with Susan's priorities throughout the novels. In LWW, for instance, she refuses to entertain Lucy's experience even after Professor Kirke (a "grown-up") suggests she should. Indeed, upon arriving in Narnia, she more than once desires to go back, even wishing to abandon Mr. Tumnus to the White Witch. Susan didn't simply "mature" out of Narnia — it's all rooted in something deeper, and Prince Caspian gives us a clue as to what that is. Here, Susan is famously the last one to see Aslan, refusing again to believe Lucy; even worse, she makes a fuss when the others do. Looking back, it's hard to see all this as anything but foreshadowing for The Last Battle. While Lewis does show us a Susan who embraces her queenly role in A Horse and His Boy, she loses sight of who she was and who crowned her when back on Earth.

Susan always struggled with faith. In Prince Caspian, she confides to Lucy that she "really believed" all along that Aslan had been calling them — or, more accurately, as she admits, "I could have, if I let myself." As Aslan soon tells her, she allowed fear to cloud her faith, keeping her from trusting what she could not see. In the case of The Last Battle, we can't fully know why she chose to reject Narnia. Perhaps it was in fear of seemingly losing Aslan again like before. Of course, if this were the case, one would suspect that Peter, Digory, or Polly (all the eldest of the Friends) would have wrestled with these same fears. Instead, Lewis leans into Susan's pre-established dispositions, perhaps being more true to her character than readers would have preferred.

At the end of The Voyage of the Dawn Treader — in which Susan does not appear — Aslan reveals to Edmund, Lucy, and Eustace the entire point of their fantasy adventures: "...by knowing me here for a little, you may know me better there." This was Lewis' in-text revelation that Aslan was meant to be a "supposal" of how Jesus Christ might appear in another world. In a sense, Narnia was a "spiritual training ground" for the Pevensies, meant to teach them how to fully recognize Christ in their world. As the character who most struggles with the notion of faith (i.e., believing without always seeing), Susan became swept up in unbelief, and thus was unable to grasp the deeper truths of Narnia. For her, "growing up" wasn't really about having more "mature experiences," but a way to escape the pain of losing those years she spent elsewhere.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

While Peter declares with sorrow that Susan is “no longer a friend of Narnia,” that does not mean she’s been rejected by Aslan as an outcast forever. The book leaves her fate uncertain, but Lewis always believed her story continued. In a 1957 letter collected in C.S. Lewis’ Letters to Children, the author states: “She is left alive in this world at the end, having by then turned into a rather silly, conceited young woman. But there's plenty of time for her to mend, and perhaps she will get to Aslan's Country in the end . . . in her own way.” Lewis would not have cared so little for Susan as to leave her in complete hopelessness. Perhaps, by removing her family from the picture, he was giving her the opportunity to finally reflect on her life and choose faith for herself, finding Aslan through her grief — something Lewis, who would later pen A Grief Observed, knew quite a bit about.

In a 1960 letter recorded in The Collected Letters of C.S. Lewis, the author admits that he couldn't write this story himself. “Not that I have no hope of Susan’s ever getting to Aslan’s Country," he explained, "but because I have a feeling that the story of her journey would be longer and more like a grown-up novel than I wanted to write.” Instead, he encouraged readers to write that story themselves. As Stuart Hunt of Into the Wardrobe points out, Lewis famously struggled with his faith. Though he was raised Anglican, he rejected religion entirely in his younger years before returning to Christianity in his early 30s (with the help of his friend J.R.R. Tolkien). Understanding this, it appears that the author's intent was never to push Susan aside, but to express a part of himself in her that simply could not be explored in these seven books — something many would relate to as they, too, grew up.

Susan Pevensie may be the most tragic character in The Chronicles of Narnia, but she is certainly not without hope. After all, as even Lewis himself once said, "When I became a man I put away childish things, including the fear of childishness and the desire to be very grown up." Of course, we can always fall back on Aslan's own words: "Once a king or queen in Narnia, always a king or queen."

Narnia: The Magician's Nephew hits theaters in 2027.

#3512. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, and it reintroduces the all-new Health app that was first available for testing during the iOS 27.2 beta. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.3 will launch with an upgraded Apple Health app. The new app was initially tested during the iOS 27.2 beta, but it’s back today in iOS 27.3 beta 1 and will ship to all users next month.

Today on Apple Newsroom, the company outlined what to expect from the new Health experience.

Three central new Health features are highlighted for iOS 27.3:

Insights tab: “surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. Longevity tab: “analyzes longitudinal metrics across heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement, metabolic health, hearing, and nutrition. Central to this tab is Health Age, a feature that translates data from Apple Watch — including VO2 max, resting heart rate, sleep, and heart rate variability — into a metric that reflects how a user’s body is tracking relative to their chronological age. Users can also incorporate clinical laboratory data, such as A1c and LDL cholesterol, to enrich their long-term health picture.”

At-home movement evaluations: “make physical assessments accessible without requiring specialized equipment. Using an iPhone camera and Apple Watch, users can measure their flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics, and VO2 max with real-time audio and visual feedback. Powered by on-device vision-based AI models and developed with clinical experts, the experience runs entirely on device; no video is ever recorded, stored, or shared.“

Additionally, Apple says that the new Health app offers expanded language support. It is available in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

#3509. iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari

Apple just released the first betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, with some big changes to Safari. The updates add a new vertical tab layout, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

#3508. Steam Officially Drops 5 More Free Games You Can Keep Forever (November 7)

Steam is the best friend to any gamer on a budget. The platform doesn't offer just games that are cheap, it also has a slew of totally free titles for anyone curious to try. Price doesn't always equate to quality when it comes to PC gaming, and there's no harm in trying a free game or two to pass the time. There are always some surprises in store, and the cost couldn't be lower.

Some of the free games on Steam this month are more than worth playing, especially considering their zero-dollar price point. Some horror titles are still slipping through the cracks after October, but there's plenty else available for free on the platform this month. Five of the games made free this week in particular might be more gamers' cup of tea than others, and the only loss in playing them is a little time and hard drive space.

This week, free-to-play gamers can look forward to an mech-based arena shooter, a comedy RPG, an incremental idle game, and more to entertain themselves on a budget.

The first free game on offer is Voltgate, a fast-paced arena shooter with a twist: players can customize their own robots and take to the arena. Voltgate has PvP for two to four players, as well as a four-player co-op wave survival mode called Headliner. This arena shooter should be a quick pick-up for those who want something quick, chaotic, and free to play with their friend group.

Townlet is the next notable free entry this week. A taskbar town idler, Townlet changes and grows based on the types of files you delete and send to your Recycle Bin. This is an interesting gimmick, but not as destructive of one as it seems. Players can simply delete something and watch their villagers grab it and take it away, then restore the file. Townlet is a very low-interaction entry to the idler genre.

Den: A Short Horror Story released in the tail-end of October but deserves a mention. Short and not-so-sweet, Den offers a short camping horror story that one can finish in a single sitting. Those still riding the horror wave will want to try this surprisingly immersive free game.

The fourth free game featured this week is WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones, which is tie-in game for the Wendy's fast food restaurants. WendyQuest is a surprisingly long and well-made game, with some players taking up to 12 hours to complete this fast food JRPG packed with personality. It's more than a little goofy, which is just what Wendy would want for her own video game.

Last but certainly not least this week is Massive Army Battle. Akin to Totally Accurate Battle Simulator but with hald-drawn sprites, Massive Army Battle offers 12 levels to play as well as one-on-one PvP. The base game is available for free and has plenty of gameplay on its own, and there is a paid Sandbox DLC to add Sandbox mode, six new heroes, and more. The base game is fun enough on its own, and costs absolutely nothing to play.

These five free Steam games may not be able to hold a candle to this season's big releases, but any one of them might be just the thing for a gamer on a budget to pass the time this month.

#3507. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.

Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $129, 46% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. The DeWalt 12-volt cordless powered ratchet is on sale at Lowe’s for $99, 50% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a DeWalt 12-volt battery and charger to use it. The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $336.19, 36% off its regular price. This is a tool only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3502. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3501. Forget 'Se7en,' Jake Gyllenhaal's Apple TV Thriller 'Prisoners' Is Even Better

A 150-minute-plus, dark-as-night kidnapping thriller isn't an instant recipe for box office success, yet Denis Villeneuve's 2013 film Prisoners handily made almost three times its budget back, while also landing on numerous year-end Top 10 lists. And the sprawling, dour crime film is still proving to have legs, as it's currently rocketing up the charts on Apple TV.

While Prisoners doesn't have any actual supernatural elements, Villeneuve and master cinematographer Roger Deakins (Blade Runner 2049, The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford) conjure such an enveloping atmosphere of menace that when villainous characters who may actually be related to a Satanic cult are introduced, it doesn't come as much of a shock at all. The film is long, unpleasantly themed, and generally hopeless. It's also a modern masterpiece, and currently receiving its due ahead of Villeneuve's eagerly anticipated Dune Part Three.

The story of Prisoners actually dates back to 2009, when Aaron Guzikowski penned a script based on his own short story, making that year's Black List. It was shopped around to stars and directors, reportedly including Leonardo DiCaprio and Antoine Fuqua, before landing in the capable hands of Denis Villeneuve. Fresh off the critically acclaimed (and extremely dark) dramatic thrillers Polytechnique and Incendies, Villeneuve proved the perfect match for the story of suburban Connecticut dad Keller Dover (Hugh Jackman), whose young daughter, along with his neighbor's child, vanishes into thin air on a chilly Thanksgiving. While Jake Gyllenhaal's Detective Loki works the case, Dover takes matters into his own hands.

Prisoners takes on an even darker tone once Dover becomes convinced that a young man with an intellectual disability, played masterfully by Paul Dano, is the culprit and takes matters into his own hands. Torture, amateur investigation, false leads, and an apparent occult kidnapping conspiracy dating back decades take over the final half, as the film keeps viewers' hearts pounding for over two and a half hours.

The story of Prisoners is fairly standard kidnapping thriller material (until it takes some dark and, arguably, unnecessary turns toward the occult and conspiratorial), but it's elevated by the sheer mood and craft that Villeneuve and Deakins bring to its world. The opening disappearance sequence is a perfect model of grey, chilly suburban banality that's nevertheless suffused with menace. Deakins lights abandoned buildings, streetlights, and parking lots like they're nestled somewhere within one of Dante's seven layers of hell. Lighting aside, Deakins' still, observational frames at time evoke another all-timer of a thriller featuring Gyllenhaal, Zodiac.

And frankly, despite its rather conventional story beats, Prisoners is rivaled by precious few American thrillers of the past several decades, including Zodiac, The Silence of the Lambs, and Se7en, a film from which it apparently borrows much of its hopeless, Satanic atmosphere. Jackman's role has been turned into a meme by many at this point, but his anguished father is actually astonishingly visceral work. In the film's famous torture sequence, in which Dover tries in vain to get information out of Dano's intellectually disabled suspect, Jackman reportedly improvised a few brutal swings of his hammer — with one landing so close to Dano's head it legitimately terrified the actor and caused him to cower to the floor.

Standing proudly alongside Se7en and The Silence of the Lambs as a potboiler elevated to high art through the magic of cinematic craftsmanship, Prisoners remains a compelling rewatch today. It's no wonder audiences are flocking to it on Apple TV.

As it did in 2025, Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on November 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart says that you can expect discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.
