#3497. iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

iOS 27.3 has just entered beta testing and includes major new features for Siri AI across iPhone, iPad and Mac. The company has unlocked many new capabilities across major Apple apps, like Music, Messages, Safari, Reminders and more.

We are still digging into the beta, but here’s a taste of what new things you can get Siri AI to do:

With the Music app, you can now create playlists and save them to your library, like you can ask it to make you “a playlist for songs for a day at the beach”, and then save it for later.

In Messages, you can now ask it to schedule iMessages to be sent later, edit and unsent messages, as well as respond with emoji reactions. You can compose new Notes with bold, italic, and rich text formatting, organize your Notes folders, and more.

Photos gets a big expansion with new Siri AI capabilities that let you favorite photos, rotate and edit images, and rename people and pets all with your voice.

You can now use Siri AI with the Calendar app to create events featuring invitees, location, video call links and more. And in Reminders, you can now create urgent reminders for the first time with Siri.

In Safari, you can now use Siri to create tap groups from a list of URLs, sort your tabs, clear your history, delete reading list items and more.

Journal support with Siri AI is new for the first time. You can create entries with text transcription, or record audio entries.

There’s also wide support for file and folder management with Siri AI Files integration. You can get file content, create files and folders, send files to the trash, organize by type, rename files, and more, using just your voice.

We are also seeing new Siri features for Weather, Maps, Preview and Shortcuts, and will keep testing to find new integrations. Apple is also opening up this support to third-party developers.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing and will be released publicly later this year.

#3496. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3494. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3490. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, one of its exclusive new features was a redesigned StandBy experience with new clock faces and expanded customization options.

#3485. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3479. Apple now explicitly bans employees from using confidential information in prediction markets

Apple has updated its insider trading policy to explicitly prohibit employees from using confidential information to bet on prediction markets. Here are the details.

Following yesterday’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings report, Apple today published its fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, which is a mandatory annual filing with the SEC that provides a detailed look at the company’s finances, business, and risks.

Among the documents included in the filing is an updated version of Apple’s insider trading policy.

Until last year, Apple’s insider trading policy, filed with the SEC as Exhibit 19.1, included the following prohibitions:

However, the updated policy includes a new prohibition:

No Trading in Prediction Markets Based on Confidential Information. Do not participate in “prediction markets” or similar platforms to wager, bet, trade, buy or sell contracts based on the outcome of future events, or otherwise enter into event contracts, when such activity involves the use of Apple Confidential Information (as defined in Apple’s Business Conduct Policy) about Apple or any other company (including Apple suppliers, manufacturers, vendors or customers, such as cellular network carriers or other business partners) obtained in connection with your work at Apple. You must also not tip Apple Confidential Information to others who may participate in such markets. Apple Confidential Information includes, but is not limited to, material nonpublic information. This prohibition applies whether or not the activity constitutes insider trading or securities trading under applicable laws.

While much of this may seem obvious, how insider trading rules apply to prediction markets has been something of a gray area, to put it mildly. And while major prediciton markets explicitly ban the practice in their terms of service, enforcement remains a challenge.

In Apple’s case, the new language explicitly extends restrictions beyond traditional securities trading, making it clear that employees cannot use confidential information to place bets on prediction markets, even when those transactions don’t qualify as insider trading under applicable laws.

You can read Apple’s full 2026 Form 10-K on its Investor Relations page.

#3478. macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look

Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

What a journey for Markdown, @gruber The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

To learn more about Markdown, follow this link.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

#3475. Willi Carlisle Says Life Is Dead Serious, Life Is a Joke on the Brilliant ‘Universal Bubba’

This week, states that most people never imagined could ever turn blue did just that, as part of a massive Democratic sweep in the midterm elections. Most people, that is, except for the residents actually living in them. Texas, Kansas, Iowa, possibly even Mississippi. No place is a monolith, and our country is a rich, vibrant, and diverse place in every corner, where real people rarely line up with the stereotypes we thrust upon them. They may not all be Instagram-glamorous, but they believe in meaningful work, family (chosen, born or both), and a good joke. They love hard, they struggle, and they get shit done.

That’s who Willi Carlisle, the Kansas-born country songwriter, is singing about on his new Tyler Childers-produced double album, The Universal Bubba. It’s the place he is writing from, the stories he tells with equal parts craft, tenderness, and a lot of humor, and it proves that celebrating our differences is what helps us live in harmony. “I sing America old and weird, wide open borders and pioneers,” Carlisle sings on “The Universal Bubba, Part Two,” one of a pair of glorious Southern rockers. “Sing on a doubleshift ‘til I’m outta breath, a song about freedom, a song about death.”

America old and weird is the story of the brilliant Universal Bubba. It’s folk songs for the people in the Ozarks and Appalachia and hollers in between who get their story sung thanks to Carlisle’s endlessly vibrant mind. Recorded in a makeshift studio in the Bywater District of New Orleans with Childers and members of his ace band, the Food Stamps, The Universal Bubba feels both otherworldly and hilariously real, maybe because so many of us can easily be both things at once. You can explore Eastern religion and still top your yerba mate with a splash of bourbon on “Marlboro Vinyasa,” but you better be able to laugh at the absurdity. You can love your country but still think it’s brutal as hell as he does on “Master’s Hammer,” a folk offering to any wayward souls ready to rip it all up and start anew. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“I’m filled with grief, but I’m wild enough to win,” Carlisle sings as the harmonies ring like a wavelength we can all tap into to, humming out of the darkness. None of these things are actually paradoxes, unless you think people can’t be complex, strange, surprising. Carlisle sure as hell does, and he wants them all to shine. Trending Stories A Jesuit Priest Explains How He Facilitated Bob Dylan’s Meeting With the Pope Appeals Court Says Lawsuit Over ‘The Pitt’ Can Proceed, Cites ‘Numerous’ Similarities to ‘ER’ Adam Lambert on His Future With Queen, New Music, and Why the Show Must Go On Pink Floyd Mark ‘Animals’ 50th Anniversary With Reissue Featuring Unreleased Music

The Universal Bubba was the first time that the equally complex and probing Childers has produced a record other than his own, and it’s a delightfully perfect fit: the two artists met while Carlisle was on tour supporting Childers in Australia, and they quickly found a musical and spiritual kinship. Carlisle is a skilled picker, but he he’s not married to tradition — nor does it feel like he’s trying to intentionally escape from it either. Banjo and fiddle (on one song, “Bigger’n Dallas,” via Amanda Shires) are the record’s heart, but never its casing. It grooves, swings, it dances to the accordion on “Old Milwaukee Onestep.” And it all ends at the Chinese food buffet.

“I wish you luck and health in business, in passion and divorce/I wish you imitation crab, wish you moo-shoo-pork,” Carlisle sings on his end-of-life prayer “Golden Dragon Buffet,” where his last request is to be sliced up and tossed in a pile of fried rice. It’s both absurd and heartbreaking, but maybe he has a point: How many of us spend more hours hunched over a greasy meal than we do with our fingers in the dirt? Life is dead serious, life is a total joke. Somewhere in between is what makes us human, and that’s where The Universal Bubba lingers.

Meanwhile, drama lovers get the ultimate primetime spectacle with a two-hour “Sheriff Country” and “Fire Country” crossover event, uniting Max Thieriot’s firefighters and Morena Baccarin’s deputies against one massive emergency.

That lineup should keep you plenty busy as November hits its stride. Clear your schedule and grab the popcorn — here are three newly added Paramount+ shows you need to add to your watchlist this weekend. Plus, check out the 13 new movies and shows to stream this weekend across all of the major streaming services.

What is it about? Paramount+ is inviting you to check out the chaotic world of one of the internet’s most beloved families. “Big John’s Bosh! Family” follows John “Big John” Fisher, the booming viral sensation behind the catchphrase, and his wife Charlotte, as they live their big, colorful lives. They've got a big family to match, with rising professional boxer son Johnny “The Romford Bull” Fisher, their “city boy” son William, their daughter Hetty, and a pair of grandmas affectionately known as “Fat Nan” and “Skinny Nan.” Each episode is a look at their family's world and how they're living.

Why you should watch it: If you’ve ever followed the Fishers’ feel-good videos online, this is an unfiltered look at the chaos and comedy that turned them into a global sensation. And even if you haven’t heard of the family, this is fun reality TV with a whole lot of heart.

Watch "Big John's Bosh! Family" on Paramount+ from Nov. 5

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

What is it about? Created, written by and starring British comedian Leo Reich, “It Gets Worse” is a dark sitcom about being young and broke. Reich plays Ethan, one of three university best friends, alongside Abi (Emily Fairn) and Sam (Olive Gray), who share a flat together in London. When an eviction notice threatens to change everything for them, these friends scramble to keep their lives, and their bond together, from completely falling apart. But as the show's title suggests, things rarely go their way.

Why you should watch it: Leo Reich is a fresh young voice in British comedy, and this six-episode Showtime series gives him a lot of room to breathe and showcase his acerbic tongue. If you like your comedies a little bleak and a lot clever, this is a quick and enjoyable binge you'll want to add to your watchlist.

Watch "It Gets Worse" on Paramount+ from Nov. 6

What is it about? Two of CBS’s hit dramas collide in this special two-hour crossover event. “Fire Country” follows Bode Donovan (Max Thieriot), a young convict who joins a prison firefighting program to serve out his sentence in his Northern California hometown, while its spinoff “Sheriff Country” centers on no-nonsense sheriff Mickey Fox (Morena Baccarin), who keeps the peace in the same county. This event brings the firefighters and the sheriff’s department together as both work to tackle an emergency bigger than the two of them.

Why you should watch it: This crossover lets the worlds of “Fire Country” and “Sheriff Country” fully overlap. That means a bigger, badder dose of life-or-death action the franchises do so well for the loyal fans. It also makes a great jumping-on point if you’ve been meaning to check out either show.

Watch the "Sheriff Country" and "Fire Country" crossover event on Paramount+ from Nov. 6

#3472. Adam Driver Explains ‘X-Men’ Came Along At “Right Time” After Years Of Rejecting Marvel Roles: “All Kind Of Came Together”

After years of rejected offers, Adam Driver is finally joining the MCU with Jake Schreier’s take on X-Men.

The 2x Oscar nominee recently explained that the role of Nathaniel Millbury/Mister Sinister came along at what “felt like a right time,” following several attempts on Kevin Feige‘s behalf to court the actor into joining the Marvel Studios fold.

“I was a big X-Men fan when I was a kid,” he explained on Jimmy Kimmel Live. “Me and my cousin, Tony, he would be Sabretooth and I would be Wolverine. It’s a big deal.”

Driver added, “I was a big fan. I mean, I was a fan of the other things too. But this one felt like a right time, and then it’s X-Men.” Watch on Deadline

As Kimmel noted, Feige previously revealed his “long-lived tradition” of getting on a Zoom with Driver to offer him an MCU role, only for the actor to think about it and pass on the project a few days later.

“It was really X-Men and Jake Schreier, who’s the director, his idea for it, and that it’s Kevin Feige,” explained Driver. “You know, it all kind of came together. The script is really cool.”

Following his casting announcement at D23 in August, the pressure is on for Driver. “A lot of people are going to watch it, and if it’s bad, a lot of people will see you being bad. Plus, I do’’t want to mess it up. I’m a huge fan of X-Men,” he told Kimmel.

Driver joins Christopher Abbott as Charles Xavier/Professor X, Inde Navarrette as Rogue, Maya Boyd as Storm, Kit Connor as Cyclops, Sadie Sink as Jean Grey, Samara Weaving as Emma Frost and Asa Germann as Angel.

Scheduled to premiere May 5, 2028 in theaters, Marvel tapped Schreier to direct X-Men last May after his previous MCU title Thunderbolts* premiered. Beef creator Lee Sung Jin and The Bear showrunner Joanna Calo are writing the script.

#3470. Trump Launches Triumphal Arch Website Right As Judge Blocks Construction

After his party suffered a brutal loss in the 2026 midterms, Donald Trump has tried to find solace in his attempts to remake Washington, D.C. But thanks to one federal judge, Trump is beginning to learn that exerting his will over the forces of state bureaucracy may not be as easy as it once was.

Late on Thursday, Judge Tanya Chutkan of the District of Columbia brought one of Trump’s prize beautification projects to a screeching halt, ruling that construction on Trump’s triumphal arch must be stopped pending the outcome of a combined legal case that names both Trump himself and the federal National Parks Service as defendants. The timing of Chutkan’s ruling couldn’t have been worse: As it came down, the White House was in the process of rolling out a glossy new website for the project, featuring 3D renderings and sweeping views of a grand structure that now may never actually be built.

A Monument to the American Spirit.The Military Triumphal Arch will honor the heroes who gave everything for our nation – a monumental tribute to America’s first 250 years & a symbol of the next 250.A legacy of freedom. A future without limits.📲 https://t.co/vkquwA5qGp pic.twitter.com/ucUPdw3YLL

This is not Chutkan’s first run-in with Trump or his administration. In 2023, Chutkan oversaw the criminal trial against Trump for his attempt to overturn the 2020 election, a case that was only dismissed after Trump won the presidency in 2024, on the basis that the federal government could not prosecute sitting presidents.

But she hasn’t been an unequivocal Trump opponent. The following year, in 2025, Chutkan declined to block the so-called Department of Government Efficiency from accessing federal employee data, saying that the plaintiffs trying to block DOGE’s power failed to prove the agency would cause “immediate, irreparable harm.”

On this ruling, however, she did not find any merit to what the government was arguing — and her opinion was unsparing on that count.

“Defendants also assert — belatedly — that the Arch represents ‘a generational national defense opportunity,’ and that the Arch may assist in combating or deterring assassination attempts on the President,” Chutkan wrote in her ruling. “The court appreciates the government’s significant interest in national security. But these recent and unsupported attestations of security … appear nowhere in the planning documents on which the project was reviewed and approved. Indeed, they materialized, for the first time, when Defendants filed their opposition brief last week.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

In less-legal terms, Chutkan is basically noting that, as opponents of the arch have suggested for months, Trump and his cronies made up some utter flimflam about the “security” opportunities of an enormous arch in the middle of D.C. and tried to shoehorn it through legal review. Chutkan has said in no uncertain terms that that’s not going to cut it.

“The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission’s decision to fully approve President Trump’s historic vision to build a much-needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C.,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle posted after the ruling. “An activist district court thereafter blocked the construction of the project.”

The judge’s posture toward the flimsy legal work of the Trump administration mirrors that of another federal judge, Ana C. Reyes, who exploded at administration lawyers in court a few weeks back after they tried to pull a fast one on her during Trump’s renovation of the East Potomac Golf Links. Reyes’ beef with the administration was more explicit — she accused them of explicitly betraying her trust — but similar to the core of Chutkan’s argument here. In essence, the administration’s lawyers can’t be trusted because they are making up whatever excuse they can to enact the president’s will.  Trending Stories A Jesuit Priest Explains How He Facilitated Bob Dylan’s Meeting With the Pope Appeals Court Says Lawsuit Over ‘The Pitt’ Can Proceed, Cites ‘Numerous’ Similarities to ‘ER’ Adam Lambert on His Future With Queen, New Music, and Why the Show Must Go On Pink Floyd Mark ‘Animals’ 50th Anniversary With Reissue Featuring Unreleased Music

Trump is, as we all know, someone who is used to getting what he wants. For his entire career, he has employed legal teams to help him accomplish those things, whether they be sweeping aside sexual assault allegations, dodging taxes, or finding ways to enrich himself from the Oval Office. Federal judges have been less amenable to this than the private courts Trump worked with as a civilian, but now, with Trump’s mandate across the government eroding by the hour, it seems unlikely any justice with a gavel is going to allow him an inch.

That won’t stop him trying, of course, as it’s very likely that building an arch or an unnecessary ballroom is the only solace he has left.

#3467. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars Toward Live-Action Foreign-Language Record $30M-$33M Opening At Domestic Box Office

FRIDAY PM UPDATE: Gkids’ Godzilla Minus Zero looks to be coming in at its opening range of $30 million-$33 million after a $13.5M Friday at 3,254 theaters that includes $6.7M in previews. At that level, that’s not only the biggest-ever opening for distributor Gkids, but it also would be the biggest opening for a live-action foreign-language movie at the domestic box office. It would overtake the 2002 Chinese movie Hero, which bowed to $17.8M. Fantastic.

Saturday will dictate if there’s a further expanded audience for the Takashi Yamazki-directed movie.

Second place goes to Warner Bros Animation’s The Cat in the Hat with a $5M Friday (including $1M previews) and a three-day total between $17M-$20M at 4,003 theaters. Critics are saying scat to the cat at 48% Rotten on Rotten Tomatoes. Watch on Deadline

Angel Studios’ colonial period feature Drummer Boy at 2,850 theaters is third with a $3.8M Friday and $9M opening.

A24’s You Can See Everything, booked at 2,473 screens, is seeing a fourth weekend between $8M-$9M in fourth place, -25%, for a running cume of $79.6M not the high end. Today is around $3.2M.

Sony’s release of Prime Focus Studios’ Ramayana: Rise of the Legend at 1,433 theaters is fifth with $6M over three days, $9M over four days.

Outside the top five is Searchlight’s Wild Horse Nine at 1,110 theaters, with $2.3M today and around $5M-$6M. That is around what Wicker debuted at ($5.7M) at 1,471 locations two weeks ago.

FRIDAY AM UPDATE: Gkids’ release of Toho’s Godzilla Minus Zero is higher with $6.7M in previews since Tuesday. As we told you that beats a slews of previews, including Legendary’s Godzilla: King of the Monsters, last year’s Predator: Badlands, but also another big Japanese title here, Pokemon: Detective Pikachu at $5.7M. Granted, it was a PG movie to Godzilla Minus Zero‘s R, but that pic posted a $20.5M first day and $54.3M opening back in mid-May 2019.

A $30M opening was considered the high end for Godzilla Minus Zero heading into the weekend and now it looks like it’s the low end. The audience score is huge at 96% on Rotten Tomatoes.

Sony Pictures’s release of Prime Focus Studios’ Ramayana: Rise of a Legend grossed $3.5 million on Thursday from 1,433 locations (including Wednesday previews), marking the widest North American release for an Indian film. Sony still thinks the movie, which is part of a $420M-$500M two part feature, is bound for a $6M opening. The pic, released in time for Diwali, currently holds a 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes’ Popcornmeter.

Warner Bros’ The Cat in the Hat came in right where it was at last night with $1M in previews.

Searchlight’s previews (both Thursday and early access) for Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine are at a great $900K. That’s not far from what Paramount/Miramax’s Roofman did last year in previews which was $1M before an $8.1M opening (though that pic was uber wide at 3,362 theaters). Wild Horse Nine is booked in 1,100 theaters.

PREVIOUS EXCLUSIVE, Thursday PM: Takashi Yamazaki’s R-rated Godzilla Minus Zero is roaring in the November box office to a great start with what we’re hearing is around $6 million in previews. That includes fan shows from Godzilla Day Tuesday, last night and tonight, the latter being $4M+. Today’s showtimes began at 10AM.

It’s very interesting that Godzilla Minus Zero gets an R: There aren’t any lizards who get naked in the movie, nor does any person or monster have a ‘F’ bomb tirade despite massive destruction in Japan as Godzilla and Ghidorah.

This is easily a preview record for Godzilla Minus Zero U.S. distributor GKIDs beating their previous high, 2023’s The Boy and the Heron which posted a Thursday and early access previews of $2.39M, and a 3-day of $13M. Early monies here on Godzilla Minus Zero are way above the $2.1M made by Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus One from its Wednesday and Thursday showtimes which went on to an $11.4M opening.

The industry forecast on the high end was $30M+ in North America for Godzilla Minus Zero, which is boosted by Imax and a ton of PLFs, but now it could be way higher when you look at the comps that the sequel is beating.

Last year at this time, Disney kicked off November with Predator: Badlands with $4.8M in Wednesday and Thursday previews which yielded a $15.8M Friday and $40M opening. Godzilla Minus Zero in previews is very close to another U.S. Godzilla, Legendary’s 2019 Godzilla: King of the Monsters which posted $6.3M in Thursday previews on its way to a $19.4M Friday and $47.7M opening. Legendary has the rights from Toho to make any English-language version from the Godzilla universe. Godzilla Minus Zero is 91% certified fresh to Godzilla Minus One‘s 99% fresh with critics. That Oscar winning movie landed an A CinemaScore. The only other Godzilla to receive a solid A was Legendary’s Godzilla vs. Kong in 2021 (2024’s Godzilla x King roared an A-).

In Japan, Godzilla Minus Zero is up to 1.38 billion yen or $8.7M and that’s through three days. That opening Godzilla Day gross of 910M yen ($5.7M) is indeed a record for a live-action pic in Japan, besting the opening day of Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (840M yen).

Warner Bros Pictures Animation’s net $86M production of The Cat in the Hat from filmmakers Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja is looking like $1M today after previews that began at 2PM. That’s on par with Sony Pictures Animation’s Goat which opened earlier this year and went on to open to $27.7M. Illumination/Universal’s The Grinch posted $2.2M in previews before a $67.5M opening weekend during the second frame of November 2018. Note, Cat in the Hat is one of the few family movies around this holiday season next to Disney’s girl-skewing Hexed which bows on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving.

#3466. Nick Cave Will Now Be Answering Your Questions in Person

Nick Cave is ready to answer your questions. On an upcoming solo tour, billed as Conversations With Nick Cave, the singer-songwriter will field questions from the audience about anything and everything — a format he works well with, as his popular Red Hand Files newsletter has shown. As with previous “Conversations” tours, the artist will also perform songs with only his own piano accompanying him.

“Years ago, in a peculiar state of mind, I travelled across the U.S., stepped onto stages in different cities, and fielded questions from the audience,” Cave said in a statement. “It was a strange, almost desperate idea, but those nights became deeply healing for me. I hope the audience felt the same.

“Eight years have passed,” he continued. “The Red Hand Files have grown in reach and stature; the topics of conversation have broadened, and it feels like the right time to return to America, a different America from eight years ago, and bring the Conversations… show back. I’ll have my piano with me, play some songs, and answer questions. What could possibly go wrong?”

Tickets go on sale to the general public on at 10 a.m. local time, Nov. 13. Presales begin Wednesday. Full details are on a bespoke website.

When Cave embarked on his first “Conversations With … ” tour in 2018, the audience’s questions prompted him to open up about some surprising things, at least for the New Yok audience: He wasn’t against people taking cell-phone photos of them, he was open to reuniting with former Bad Seed Blixa Bargeld (the reunion still hasn’t happened), and meeting Johnny Cash was a revelation. He also told the crowd that speaking with them helped him with his grief after the death of his son. “Talking to the audience has actually been extraordinary healing for me,” he said. #3465. How to get access to Sonos AI features, as company aims to avoid another app disaster

When Sonos tried a major app update two years ago, things did not go well. Much-loved features disappeared, older speakers experienced connection problems, and accessibility features were broken. That debacle saw the company’s CEO fired.

The company is taking a much more cautious approach as it moves into the AI era with a Sonos 27voice update, enabling natural-language voice control via Hey Sonos requests …

The whole mess started when Sonos launched the company’s first headphones, the Ace, intended to compete with AirPods Max. The app needed to be updated to support these, and the company decided to use it as an opportunity for a ground-up rebuild, launching a completely new app just ahead of the launch.

Customers responded angrily to the loss of key functionality, compatibility issues with older speakers, and accessibility problems. Sonos initially downplayed the complaints, but CEO Patrick Spence subsequently emailed customers to apologize, and provide a timeline for fixes, subsequently making seven promises. However, customers weren’t impressed, and called for Spence to be fired – later getting their wish.

This time around, Sonos started out with a modest update in the form of the Sonos 27 app, leaving the more substantial changes to a subsequent Sonos 27voice version. This will replace the more limited voice control available today, much like the update from old Siri to Siri AI.

Rather than pushing it out to all customers, Sonos is adopting a very cautious approach. First, you’ll have to request early access to the beta and be approved. Second, the company is testing the feature with a relatively small group of users. Third, it’s seeking detailed feedback from beta testers before a planned launch next year.

The new features work in much the same way as Siri on HomePods.

You can use Sonos 27voice at any time by saying the wake word, “Hey Sonos.” While Sonos is listening, the white status light on your Sonos product will glow brighter and the volume will lower if any audio is playing. A confirmation tone will play after Sonos understands your request.

The company says you can then use natural language for both music-related commands and information searches. The company gives the following music examples:

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: Think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, but prices aren’t always what they seem. Use a price tracker to make sure you’re getting the best deal, or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3460. Apple still charging 300% of costs on iPhone storage upgrades, says WSJ

Opting for more RAM or storage when buying Apple devices has always been an expensive business, with the company famously charging huge markups.

Apple said in its most recent earnings report that even after the price increases, its margins are being squeezed by higher component costs. But an analysis suggests that the company is still charging three times its own costs for higher storage tiers on the iPhone 18 Pro …

To be fair to Apple, some of the criticism about the premiums charged on configuring a device with more memory or flash storage hasn’t been comparing, well, apples with apples. The SSDs used in Macs, for example, are very much faster than the lower-spec third-party storage cards people typically cite as evidence for the company’s greed.

why are people defending Apple? They are bending everybody over double to keep their profit margins. They buy a billion memory chips or SSD's at a time so they are getting them much lower in price even if the price has gone up.

All the same, there’s no denying that the iPhone maker has always applied extremely high markups to its own direct costs. With the iPhone 17 Pro, for example, upgrading from 256GB to 1TB cost a buyer $400. A Wall Street Journal analysis cited by Macworld says that Apple’s cost at the time was $42, almost a 1,000% markup.

Apple this week warned that memory costs will reduce its holiday quarter profit margins.

When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon.

However, the WSJ’s number-crunching suggests that we probably don’t need to get out the violins just yet. The paper compared the same upgrade on the iPhone 18 Pro, where Apple has increased the price difference to $600. Although the Cupertino company is paying dramatically more, with an estimated direct cost of $192, that still amounts to customers being charged more than three times the price paid by Apple.

#3458. Trump’s First Big Post-Midterms Move Is Promoting Stephen Miller

What do you do when the entire country tells you, in unmistakable and politically apocalyptic terms, that they are tired of your shit? If you’re Donald Trump, you are likely incapable of doing anything other than doubling down on your worst impulses, and that’s exactly what the president did on Friday.

In his first major political move since Republicans’ annihilation in the 2026 midterm elections, Trump has announced that he will be promoting Stephen Miller — the architect of some of his most inhumane and unpopular policies — to White House Chief of Staff, replacing Susie Wiles, who had served in the role since Trump retook office last year. Miller had been serving as the Deputy Chief of Staff prior to his promotion this week.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. He added that Wiles “will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

In a statement released on social media, Wiles confirmed that she would be ceding her post, adding that while her “role may be changing,” her “commitment to the President and the mission never will.” It’s not clear exactly what the “Trump Political Operation” is, and what Wiles role will be within it.

The outgoing chief of staff, a longtime political consultant credited with orchestrating much of the president’s 2024 campaign strategy, announced earlier this year that she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer, and received successful treatment over the summer.

Miller has been the face and voice of the most extreme wing of the MAGA-aligned right for years. He has long espoused white nationalism, and was the mastermind behind the Trump administration’s family separation policy during the president’s first term, and of the racist, xenophobic crackdowns on immigration and communities of color that have defined Trump 2.0.  Trending Stories A Jesuit Priest Explains How He Facilitated Bob Dylan’s Meeting With the Pope Appeals Court Says Lawsuit Over ‘The Pitt’ Can Proceed, Cites ‘Numerous’ Similarities to ‘ER’ Adam Lambert on His Future With Queen, New Music, and Why the Show Must Go On Pink Floyd Mark ‘Animals’ 50th Anniversary With Reissue Featuring Unreleased Music

As previously reported by Rolling Stone, it was Miller who pressed the administration to set absurd quotas for migrant arrests and deportations, moved to revoke civil protections and due process rights from detainees, and exerted effective control over the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security.

Miller has vociferously defended the actions of the administration at every turn. In the aftermath of an election in which voters across the political spectrum made clear the politics of divisiveness, violence, and self aggrandizement peddled by current White House leadership are not serving them, one would hope there would be at least a few days of introspection — or at least of shrewd political strategizing to mitigate downstream losses. Instead Trump is handing even more power and influence to one of his most controversial advisers, and Americans will continue to suffer for it.

Given the long-term energy savings of LED bulbs compared to conventional incandescent and fluorescent options, it might be worth grabbing a couple. Here’s why.

The GE LED+ A21 LED Light Bulb Color Changing Bluetooth Speaker lets you play music directly from your phone to it, making it the perfect bedside companion when you're trying to wind down. In addition, it comes with a remote that easily lets you change its colors, intensity, and even set up a multi-unit system for stereo sound.

What really sold me on this setup is that it’s not trying to compete with all the other speakers I have around, including the two Apple HomePods in my bedroom that I use with my TV. While the sound isn’t mind-blowing, it’s more than enough to help me wind down before bedtime. Since the bulb sits in a lamp right next to my bed, it’s perfect for playing ambient noise or an audiobook to help me fall asleep. That same balance also makes it a solid upgrade for a home office, delivering background music while working.

It’s also worth highlighting that despite its color-changing abilities, this isn’t technically a "smart" bulb that relies on Wi-Fi — and you don’t need to download another app. Instead, it pairs with a simple remote that lets me cycle through colors, tweak brightness, and adjust audio playback with the click of a physical button. This plug-and-play simplicity makes it super easy to use and ideal for older adults or elderly family members who don’t want the hassle of complicated tech.

The reason I suggest getting a pair isn’t just the extra savings — it’s that you can link multiple bulbs together completely wire-free. I’ve set it up so the two light bulbs sit on opposite sides of my bed, assigning one as the left channel and the other as the right. Effectively, I get a true stereo pair that makes listening far more immersive. There’s also a Party Mode that syncs the bulbs to change colors and pulse to the beat of the music.

Between its simple remote controls, clutter-free audio, and wire-free stereo pairing, this two-in-one bulb convinced me it’s no gimmick — especially while you can grab it for just $22 for a limited time.

#3454. With iOS 27.3, Apple will start checking iCloud public links for ‘harmful content’

iOS 27.3 adds lots of new iPhone features, and it also makes a change to how public iCloud links work with the aim of preventing harmful content from being shared. Here are the details.

This week Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta, which adds Siri AI improvements, new Safari features, the all-new Apple Health app, and more.

Per a newly published support document on Apple’s website, iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and more also include a key change to how iCloud public links work.

Apple currently provides two main options when sharing photos, files, and more via iCloud. You can share with ‘People you choose’ or create a public link that works for ‘Anyone with the link.’

Starting with iOS 27.3 and companion updates, the ‘Anyone with the link’ option will start being checked by Apple for harmful content.

When you share content that’s stored in iCloud, such as a photo in iCloud Photos or a file in iCloud Drive, you can choose to Share a Link or Send a Copy of the item. If you choose Share a Link, you can either share the item with “People you choose” — only people you invite or approve — or with “Anyone with the link,” which makes it accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple. Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content.

If Apple flags the content you’re sharing as harmful, the support doc says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time.”

I’m okay with Apple doing this. HOWEVER, they should publish at least rough guidelines on what they will consider “harmful”.

Saying nothing more than “harmful” leaves way too much open to arbitrary interpretation.

For anyone trying to upload harmful content, the company may “take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement.”

As outlined above, choosing the ‘Anyone with the link’ option has always made it accessible to “anyone who has the link, including Apple.” That’s because it’s a public link.

What’s changing now, though, is that Apple says it will begin checking those public links for harmful content.

Do you use iCloud public links? What’s your take on this change? Let us know in the comments.

#3453. Tegan and Sara Celebrate the Season With ‘I Love Christmas’ and ‘A December to Remember’

Tegan and Sara are getting into the holiday spirit with not one, but two Christmas-themed songs, “I Love Christmas” and “A December to Remember.”

In the video for “I Love Christmas” the Quin sisters acknowledge not everyone is into the holiday, but they have enough cheer to make up for those who aren’t feeling it. “I love Christmas, even if you don’t/I can love it for us, even if you won’t,” they sing on the chorus. “I love the music and the weather and the presents, too/I know you hate this time of year, it makes you blue/Let me love it for you.”

The adoration for the season is not mere talk. “I’m a Christmas fanatic. I have three Christmas trees,” she says. “I watch a Christmas movie every single day in December and listen exclusively to Christmas music.” Tegan said in a statement. “Like most sane people, I actually prefer the anticipation of Christmas to Christmas itself. By Christmas afternoon, I’m usually pretty depressed.”

For “A December to Remember,” Tegan and Sara take turns grabbing stuff from a refrigerator as they sing about wrapping gifts and watching Home Alone together, and making other joyful memories. “You work to keep my spirits bright/You know that this is the time of the year I love, so you pull out all the stops and give me a December to remember with 25 reasons to cheer” goes the chorus. The visual culminates with the sisters clad in Christmas sweaters toasting champagne.

The songs hailed from a project with Kate Cooper penned around the time of Tegan and Sara’s 2024 graphic novel, Crush. After Tegan finished penning Merry Christmess, her first middle-grade novel that arrived in September, she said that she decided to revisit the songs. #3451. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.
